children.translated_text: These are its special qualities: color, taste, smell, and touch. The others are number, magnitude, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, heaviness, occasional fluidity, and disposition.

children.text: rūpaṃ śuklādi raso madhurādiḥ gandhaḥ surabhirasurabhiśca sparśo'syā anuṣṇāśītatve sati pākajaḥ kāryaṃ bāhyam ādhyātmikaṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: Color is such as white; taste is such as sweet; smell is fragrant and non-fragrant. Its touch, being neither hot nor cold, is produced by cooking. Its effect is both external and internal.
Color, taste, and touch are respectively white, sweet, and cold.
The word "fluid" indicates natural fluidity.
"Unctuous" means that these alone have unctuousness.
And there are number, magnitude, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, heaviness, and disposition.
The effect is as before.

children.text: rūpaṃ bhāsvaraṃ śuklaṃ ca sparśa uṣṇa eva ||
children.translated_text: Its color is bright and white, and its touch is only hot.
And there are number, magnitude, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, occasional fluidity, and disposition.
The effect is as before.
Touch is neither hot nor cold and is not produced by cooking.
And there are number, magnitude, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, heaviness, and disposition.
The effect is as before.
Bodies made of earth and so on exist in the worlds of earth and so on.
Those color, taste, smell, and touch do not exist in space.
Its qualities are sound, number, magnitude, separateness, conjunction, and disjunction.
<s>Madhūcchiṣṭa</s> is wax.

children.text: sarpiṣo jatuno madhūcchiṣṭasya cāgnisaṃyogād dravatā yā saṃjāyate tad adbhiḥ samānatvaṃ pṛthivyāḥ ||
children.translated_text: The fluidity that arises in ghee, lac, and wax through conjunction with fire is earth's commonality with water.

children.text: eṣāṃ ca taijasānāṃ yadagnisaṃyogād dravatvamupajāyate tadadbhiḥ sāmānyaṃ tejasaḥ ||
children.translated_text: And the fluidity that arises in these fiery things through conjunction with fire is fire's commonality with water.
The sūtra is for the sake of an example.
"In cowhood" means an individual delimited by cowhood.

children.text: viṣāṇaṃ kakudaṃ sāsnā cāsyāstīti viṣāṇī kakudmān sāsnāvān ||
children.translated_text: Since it has a horn, a hump, and a dewlap, it is horned, humped, and dewlapped.

children.text: prāntaśabdena kaṭibhāgaḥ vālā asmin dhīyanta iti vāladhiśabdena puccham prānte vāladhirasyeti prāntevāladhiḥ ||
children.translated_text: By the word <s>prānta</s> the hip-region is meant. Since hairs are placed there, the word <s>vāladhī</s> means the tail; because its tail is at the rear, it is called <s>prāntevāladhī</s>, "having the tail at the rear."

children.text: viṣāṇyādibhiḥ śabdaistadvatpratipādakair api arthavyāpārād dharmā eva vyapadiśyante ||
children.translated_text: Even by words such as "horned," which indicate something possessing those things, the properties themselves are designated by semantic operation.

children.text: yathā apratyakṣāyāṃ govyaktau kathaṃcid gṛhyamāṇā viṣāṇādayo liṅgaṃ dṛṣṭamanumāpakās tathā ||
children.translated_text: Just as, in the case of an imperceptible individual cow, horns and the like, being somehow apprehended, are seen as marks that produce inference, so too here.
Touch, when apprehended, makes air inferred, because it is impossible for it to be without a substratum.

children.text: yadi khalvayaṃ kṣityādisparśo 'bhaviṣyad gandharasarūpaiḥ sahopalabhemahi na caivam tasmāt pṛthivyādivyatiriktasya vāyor liṅgam ||
children.translated_text: For if this were touch belonging to earth and the rest, we would apprehend it together with smell, taste, and color. But this is not so. Therefore it is a mark of air, which is distinct from earth and the rest.

children.text: yaḥ paramāṇusvabhāvo vāyuḥ sa khalvadravyavattvāt samavāyikāraṇarahitatvād dravyam ||
children.translated_text: The air that has the nature of an atom is indeed a substance, because it does not possess another substance and because it lacks an inherent cause.
For a substance is either not itself possessed of substance, or it is composed of many substances.

children.text: kriyāvad guṇavat iti dravyalakṣaṇād yatra kriyā guṇāśca samavetāḥ so'pi mahān vāyurdravyam ||
children.translated_text: And from the definition of substance as "possessing action and possessing qualities," that great air too, in which action and qualities inhere, is a substance.
The eternality of air characterized as atomic has been stated through its not possessing another substance and through its lacking an inherent cause.

children.text: tiryaggāmino vāyorvāyusaṃmūrcchanena vāyvantarasaṃśleṣeṇordhvagamanaṃ pravartate tata ūrdhvagamanāt saṃśleṣaḥ saṃśleṣād vāyoranekatvamanumīyate ||
children.translated_text: When air that moves sideways goes upward through the compacting of air, that is, through its conjunction with another air, then from that upward movement there is conjunction; from conjunction the plurality of air is inferred.
But, one may object:

children.text: yathā ayaṃ gauḥ iti goścakṣuṣā sannikarṣe sati pratyakṣeṇa viṣāṇādīni tadyogitayā dṛṣṭāni kadācilliṅgam naivaṃ tvacā vāyoḥ sannikarṣe sati ayaṃ vāyuriti pratyakṣeṇa tadguṇatayā sparśa upalabdho yenānupalabhyamānaṃ kadācid vāyumanumāpayet ||
children.translated_text: When there is contact of the eye with a cow, as in "this is a cow," horns and the like are perceived directly as belonging to it, and only sometimes become a mark. It is not like this when there is contact of the skin with air: touch is not apprehended by direct perception as a quality of it in the form "this is air," such that it might at some time make the unapprehended air inferred.

children.text: kṣityādisparśavidharmatvādasya sparśasya nirāśrayasya cābhāvād vāyurāśraya iti cet ||
children.translated_text: If it is said that, because this touch differs in property from the touch of earth and the rest, and because it cannot exist without a substratum, air is its substratum,

children.text: ākāśādīnāmapi parokṣatvāt tatpratiṣedhena vāyorevāyaṃ sparśa ityayaṃ viśeṣa etasmāt sāmānyatodṛṣṭānnāvagamyate ||
children.translated_text: then since space and the others too are imperceptible, this specific fact, namely that this is the touch of air alone through exclusion of them, is not understood from this generally observed inference.

children.text: vibhūnāṃ sparśavattve bhāvānāṃ pratighāta iti cet evaṃ tarhi vāyorevāyaṃ bhavatprasiddhasya sparśo na daśamasya dravyasyeti kathaṃ jñāyate ||
children.translated_text: If it is said that, if pervasive entities possessed touch, there would be obstruction, then how is it known that this touch belongs only to air, which is accepted by you, and not to a tenth substance?
Therefore the sentence "air exists" is scriptural, merely a traditional assertion: this is the meaning.
This is not so.

children.text: asmadādīnāṃ sakāśād yo bhagavān vijñānādibhir viśiṣṭo maheśvarastadīyaṃ saṃjñāpraṇayanaṃ navānāmeva dravyāṇāṃ bhāve liṅgam daśamasya saṃjñānabhidhānāt ||
children.translated_text: The assigning of names by that blessed <s>Maheśvara</s>, who is superior to people like us through knowledge and the like, is a mark that only nine substances exist, because no name for a tenth is stated.
Therefore there are exactly nine substances.
Hence touch belongs to air alone.
The plural in "those superior to us" is used honorifically.
How is he known? This is now stated.

children.text: pratyakṣeṇa hi padārthamālocayantaḥ saṃjñāḥ praṇayanti dṛṣṭaṃ ca dārakasya nāmakaraṇe praṇītāścemāḥ khalu saṃjñāḥ tasmānmanyāmahe asti bhagavānasmadviśiṣṭo yo'smadādi parokṣāṇāmapi bhāvānāṃ pratyakṣadarśī yenedaṃ saṃjñādi praṇītamiti ||
children.translated_text: For those who examine an object by direct perception assign names, and this is seen in the naming of a child. Now these names have indeed been assigned. Therefore we think that there exists a blessed one, superior to us, who directly sees even things imperceptible to people like us, by whom this naming and so forth was established.

children.text: yadetanniṣkramaṇaṃ praveśanaṃ ca puruṣasya dvārādinā bhavati na bhittyādau tadākāśakṛtam ato niṣkramaṇapraveśane ākāśasya liṅgamiti ||
children.translated_text: The fact that a person's going out and entering take place through a door and the like, but not through a wall and the like, is caused by space. Therefore going out and entering are the mark of space.
For space is the absence of what is corporeal.
That is not so.

children.text: niṣkramaṇādi karma puruṣe vartamānam ekadravyaṃ karma ityuktatvānniṣkriyatvāccākāśasya ākāśāvṛtti kathaṃ tad gamayed asaṃbandhāt ||
children.translated_text: Actions such as going out, occurring in a person, are said to be actions inhering in a single substance; and since <s>ākāśa</s> is inactive, how could an action not residing in <s>ākāśa</s> make that known, since there is no relation?

children.text: yathā loṣṭavṛtti patanaṃ gurutvasya liṅgamevaṃ puruṣavṛtti niṣkramaṇamākāśasya liṅgamiti cet na ||
children.translated_text: If it is said, "Just as falling, which resides in a clod, is a mark of heaviness, so going out, which resides in a person, is a mark of <s>ākāśa</s>," no.

children.text: gurutvaṃ karmaṇo'samavāyikāraṇamuktam tad anumīyatām na tvākāśasyāsamavāyikāraṇatvaṃ yujyate nityatvadravyatvānāśritatvair ākāśasya gurutvādinā asamavāyikāraṇena vaidharmyāt ||
children.translated_text: Heaviness has been stated to be a non-inherent cause of action, and so it may be inferred. But it is not reasonable that <s>ākāśa</s> should be a non-inherent cause, because <s>ākāśa</s>, being eternal, a substance, and without a substrate, is dissimilar to heaviness and the like, which are non-inherent causes.

children.text: yaduktaṃ niṣkramaṇaṃ cākāśakṛtatvād dvārādinā iti etanna ||
children.translated_text: As for what was said, "Going out is due to <s>ākāśa</s>, through a door and the like," that is not so.

children.text: bhittyādinā sparśavaddravyeṇa śarīrādeḥ karmādhārasya saṃyogānniṣkramaṇaṃ nivartate na tvākāśābhāvāt tasya sarvagatatvāt tatrāpi bhāvaḥ tasmācchabdaliṅgam evākāśam ||
children.translated_text: Going out by the body and so on, the substratum of action, is stopped by contact with a touch-bearing substance such as a wall, not by absence of <s>ākāśa</s>; since <s>ākāśa</s> is all-pervasive, it is present there too. Therefore <s>ākāśa</s> has sound alone as its mark.

children.text: bheryādīnāmeva nimittānāṃ śabdo guṇa iti cet na ||
children.translated_text: If it is said that sound is a quality of causes such as drums, no.

children.text: iha ye sparśavatāṃ viśeṣaguṇā ekaikendriyagrāhyāste kāraṇaguṇaiḥ kārye niṣpādyante ||
children.translated_text: Here, those specific qualities of touch-bearing things which are apprehended by a single sense are produced in the effect by qualities of the cause.

children.text: na ca bheryavayaveṣu rūpādaya iva kaścicchabdabhāgaḥ samaveta upalabhyate ||
children.translated_text: But no portion of sound is perceived as inhering in the parts of a drum, as color and the like are.
Therefore, because it is not preceded by a quality of the cause, sound is not a specific quality of a touch-bearing thing such as a drum.

children.text: yaśca sparśavato viśeṣaguṇaḥ sa kārye yāvatkāryamupalabhyamāno dṛṣṭaḥ ||
children.translated_text: And whatever is a specific quality of a touch-bearing thing is seen to be perceived in the effect for as long as the effect exists.

children.text: na caivaṃ śabdaḥ tato na sparśavadviśeṣaguṇaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Sound is not so. Hence it is not a specific quality of a touch-bearing thing.

children.text: kiṃca sparśavadviśeṣaguṇa ārabdhe kārye kāraṇaguṇairārabhyate na ca yadā śabdena śabda ārabhyate tadā kiṃcit kāryamutpannaṃ paśyāmaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Moreover, a specific quality of a touch-bearing thing is produced in an effect that has been begun, by qualities of the cause; but when sound is produced by sound, we do not see any effect produced.

children.text: tasmāt kāryāntarāprādurbhāvācca na śabdaḥ sparśavato viśeṣaguṇa iti ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, also because no other effect becomes manifest, sound is not a specific quality of a touch-bearing thing.
"Elsewhere" means outside.
For qualities of the self, such as pleasure and the like, are perceived within the body.
Sound is not so, because it is perceived outside by many people.

children.text: na cātmaguṇo bāhyendriyagrāhyaḥ ayaṃ tu śrotrapratyakṣaḥ tasmānnātmaguṇaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Nor is a quality of the self grasped by an external sense; but this is directly perceived by the ear. Therefore it is not a quality of the self.

children.text: ata eva bahirupalabhyamānatvād bāhyendriyapratyakṣatvācca na manoguṇaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For this very reason, because it is perceived outside and is directly perceived by an external sense, it is not a quality of the mind.
And because it is directly perceived by the ear, it is not a quality of direction or of time.
Therefore, being a quality,
therefore sound, being perceived, makes <s>ākāśa</s> known.

children.text: yathā adravyavattvāt paramāṇubhūto vāyurdravyaṃ nityaśca evamākāśaṃ kāraṇadravyābhāvād dravyaṃ nityaṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: Just as air in atomic form, because it does not possess another substance, is a substance and eternal, so <s>ākāśa</s>, because it lacks a causal substance, is a substance and eternal.

children.text: yathā salliṅgāviśeṣād viśeṣaliṅgābhāvāccaiko bhāva evaṃ śabdaliṅgāviśeṣād viśeṣaliṅgābhāvāccaikam ākāśam ||
children.translated_text: Just as, because there is no distinction among the marks of existence and because there is no special mark, existence is one only, so because there is no distinction in the mark consisting of sound and because there is no special mark, <s>ākāśa</s> is one.
Thus ends the first daily lesson of the second book.

children.text: puṣpeṇa khalu saṃyukte vastre na puṣpagandhena gandha ārabhyate vastragandhasyāpi sambhavāt puṣpavastragandhābhyāṃ dvābhyāṃ vilakṣaṇaṃ gandhāntaramupajanitamupalabhemahi na caivam api tu puṣpagandham evopalabhāmahe ||
children.translated_text: When cloth is in contact with a flower, scent is surely not produced by the flower's scent, because the cloth's own scent is also possible; for then we would perceive another scent, distinct from both the flower's scent and the cloth's scent, produced by the two scents, but that is not the case. Rather, we perceive only the flower's scent.

children.text: tasmāt anārabdhe kārye puṣpagandhena gandha ārabhyate ityayuktam gandhāntaraprasaṅgāt ||
children.translated_text: Therefore it is unreasonable that, in an effect not yet begun, scent is produced by the flower's scent, because it would entail another scent.

children.text: apāṃ tejasā saṃyoge sati vilakṣaṇasparśānutpattirauṣṇyābhāvasya liṅgam ayāvad dravyabhāvitvaṃ ca salile auṣṇyasya ||
children.translated_text: When water is in conjunction with fire, the non-production of a distinct touch is the mark of the absence of heat, and heat exists in water only as long as the substance is so conditioned.

children.text: sūkṣmāṇāṃ puṣpāvayavānāṃ vastre tejo'vayavānāṃ cāpsu saṅkrānteḥ saṃyuktasamavāyād gandhasparśopalabdhiḥ ||
children.translated_text: The perception of scent and touch occurs through conjunction with inherence, because minute parts of the flower pass into the cloth and parts of fire pass into water.

children.text: nanv ayāvad dravyabhāvino rūpādayo vastrodakayoḥ puṣpagandhoṣṇasparśopalambhakāle svagandhaśītasparśānupalabdheḥ ||
children.translated_text: Objection: Color and the other qualities in the cloth and water last only as long as the substance is so conditioned, because at the time when the flower's scent and hot touch are perceived, their own scent and cold touch are not perceived.
No.
Although its own scent remains present in an earthy cloth, it is not perceived because it is overpowered by the flower's scent.
Moreover,
heat remains in fire alone; it does not pass into water.
Likewise, at the time when heat is perceived,

children.text: tejo'vayavānupraveśāt saṃyuktasamavāyād uṣṇopalabdhāvapi anupalabhyamānāpi salile śītatā vyavasthitaivābhibhavān nopalabhyate ||
children.translated_text: even when heat is perceived because of the entry of particles of fire and through conjunction with inherence, the coldness in the water, though not being perceived, remains established; it is not perceived because it is overpowered.
Now time is being discussed.
These, such as the intermixture of posteriority and priority, are marks of time.

children.text: tatra pareṇa divapradeśena saṃyukte yūni paratvajñāne jāte sthavire cāpareṇa dikpradeśena saṃyukte'paratvajñānotpattau kṛṣṇakeśādivalīpalitādiparyālocanayā yena nimittena yūni aparatvajñānaṃ sthavire ca paratvajñānaṃ jāyate sa kālaḥ ||
children.translated_text: In this case, when a cognition of priority arises with regard to a young man connected with a more distant region of direction, and when a cognition of posteriority arises with regard to an old man connected with a nearer region of direction, then, after considering black hair, wrinkles, gray hair, and the like, that cause by which a cognition of posteriority arises in the young man and a cognition of priority in the old man is time.

children.text: tathā tulyakāryeṣu kartṛṣu yugapat kurvanti ayugapatkurvanti iti yataḥ pratyayo jāyate sa kālaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Similarly, when agents engaged in equal tasks are acting simultaneously or not acting simultaneously, that from which the cognition arises is time.

children.text: tathaikaṃ kriyāphalamuddiśya odanākhyaṃ bhūyasīnāmadhiśrayaṇādikriyāṇāṃ prabandhapravṛttau tulye kartari ciramadya kṛtam kṣipram adya kṛtam iti yataḥ pratyayau bhavataḥ sa kāla iti ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, when many actions beginning with putting on the pot proceed in sequence, with a single result of action in view, namely what is called cooked rice, and with the agent being the same, that from which the two cognitions arise, "today it was done slowly" and "today it was done quickly," is time.
Its qualities are number, magnitude, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction.
Moreover,
because it does not possess another substance, time has substantiality and eternality, like atomic air.

children.text: yathā salliṅgāviśeṣād viśeṣaliṅgābhāvāccaiko bhāvastathā kālaliṅgāviśeṣād viśeṣaliṅgābhāvāccaikaḥ kālaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Just as, because there is no difference in the marks of existence and because there is no special mark, existence is one, so too, because there is no difference in the marks of time and because there is no special mark, time is one.
If time is one, how is there the designation 'time of beginning' and so on? To this he says:

children.text: kāryaṃ kriyā kriyāviśeṣeṇāviṣṭasya vastuna ārambhasthitivināśakriyā dṛṣṭvā ekasyāpi kālasya nānātvopacārād ārambhakālādivyapadeśaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Having observed an effect, an action, and the actions of beginning, continuance, and destruction in an object possessed of a particular action, there is the designation 'time of beginning' and so on because plurality is figuratively attributed even to the one time.
Objection: mere action is time.
Why? Because of the marks of time.

children.text: yadi kriyāvyatiriktaḥ syānnityaḥ kāla evaṃ nityeṣvapyākāśādiṣu kālaliṅgāni pratibhāseran ||
children.translated_text: If time were eternal and distinct from action, then the marks of time would appear even in eternal things such as ether and the like.
But they occur only in impermanent things.
Therefore time is a limit only in things that are being produced.
Therefore action itself is time.

children.text: naitat vastunirvṛttyuttarakālabhāvitvāt kālaliṅgānyanityeṣu bhavanti na tu kriyāyāḥ kālatvāt ||
children.translated_text: This is not so. The marks of time occur in impermanent things because they come into being after the production of the object, not because action is time.
But with regard to them:

children.text: eṣāṃ kālaliṅgānāṃ nirnimittānāmasambhavāt kriyānimittatve kṛtam iti syāt na yugapat iti ||
children.translated_text: Since these marks of time cannot exist without a cause, if action were their cause, it would follow that 'it has been done' would be simultaneous; but it is not simultaneous.
Therefore the name 'time' belongs to that which is the cause of these marks.

children.text: mūrtadravyamavadhiṃ kṛtvā yata etad bhavati idamasmāt pūrveṇa ityādipratyayas tad diśo liṅgam ||
children.translated_text: Taking an embodied substance as a limit, the cognition such as 'this is east of that' arises from it; that is the mark of direction.
Its qualities are number, magnitude, separateness, conjunction, and disjunction.
Moreover:
Because, like air, it is without the property of possessing another substance, direction has substantiality and eternality.
The meaning is that, because there is no difference in the marks of direction and because there is no special mark, direction is one.
When its unity is established:

children.text: pūrveṇa devayajanaṃ dakṣiṇena pitṛyajanamityādinā kriyāviśeṣeṇa nānātvasya diśaḥ pūrvadakṣiṇāderupacāraḥ ||
children.translated_text: Through particular actions, as in 'the gods' sacrifice is to the east' and 'the ancestors' sacrifice is to the south,' plurality is figuratively attributed to direction as east, south, and so on.

children.text: savituraharādau yena kalpitadikpradeśena saṃyogo'bhūd bhavati bhaviṣyati vā tasmādādityasaṃyogāt prācī iti vyapadeśaḥ prāñcatyata ādityamiti ||
children.translated_text: From that conjunction with the sun, namely with the direction-region conventionally fixed where there was, is, or will be conjunction with the sun at the beginning of the day, the designation 'eastern' arises, because it faces toward the sun.
From this very contact with the sun comes the designation 'southern' and the rest.
In this same manner the other directions, east, south, and so forth, have been explained.
Now in that connection the self is to be apprehended by the instruments, and the instruments from the qualities such as sound and the rest.
Objection: the status of sound and the others as qualities is unproved, yet it is stated as though proved.

children.text: nanu guṇatve kutaḥ saṃśayaḥ āha kiṃ saṃśayo'pi hetumān evametat ||
children.translated_text: Objection: how can there be doubt about their being qualities? He says: Is even doubt possessed of a reason? Yes, this is so.
What is the reason? He states it:

children.text: sthāṇupuruṣayor ūrdhvatāṃ sāmānyaṃ paśyan viśeṣahetūn pāṇyādikoṭarādīn apaśyan smarati ca viśeṣān ataḥ saṃśayaḥ kimayaṃ sthāṇuḥ syāt puruṣo na vā iti ||
children.translated_text: Seeing the common property of uprightness in a stump and a man, not seeing the distinguishing causes such as hands or hollows, and remembering the distinctions, one has doubt: 'Could this be a stump, or is it a man?'
That doubt is twofold, external and internal.
The external also is twofold, perceptible and imperceptible.
First, in the case of the imperceptible:

children.text: tu prāpto manuṣya ityukte kimimaṃ dṛṣṭaṃ paśyeyamadṛṣṭamiti śravaṇamātrādeva saṃśayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: When one is told, 'A man has arrived,' doubt arises from hearing alone: 'Shall I see someone I have seen before, or someone I have not seen?'
But in the case of the perceptible:

children.text: samprati dṛṣṭvā puruṣaṃ tameva dṛṣṭamālocayataḥ kimayaṃ mayā dṛṣṭapūrvaḥ kadācidutādṛṣṭa iti saṃśayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: After seeing a man at present, as one considers that very man seen, there is doubt: 'Was this person ever seen by me before, or not seen?'

children.text: ādau kuntalī devadatto dṛṣṭaḥ madhye muṇḍaḥ tṛtīyasyāmavasthāyāṃ kuntalī ||
children.translated_text: At first <s>Devadatta</s> was seen with hair; in the middle he was shaven; in a third condition he had hair.

children.text: caturthyāmālāpādibhiravagate ārūpamātreṇa ca saṃdhyādau kim ayaṃ kuntalī syād uta muṇḍo vā iti saṃśayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: In a fourth condition, when he is recognized by conversation and the like, but only his form is visible at twilight and so on, there is doubt: 'Could this be the one with hair, or the shaven one?'
In the previous sūtra, doubt arose from the recollection of many objects; by this one, however, it arises from the recollection of distinctions in a single object.
But the internal is as follows:
Knowledge is correct cognition; ignorance is false cognition.

children.text: daivajñena śubhamādiṣṭaṃ satyamabhūt dvitīyam asatyam tṛtīyasyāmavasthāyāṃ saṃśayaḥ kim ādyāvasthāvat satyamuta dvitīyāvasthāvad asatyamiti ||
children.translated_text: A favorable prediction was made by an astrologer and turned out true; a second was false. In a third case there is doubt: 'Will it be true like the first case, or false like the second case?'
Thus doubt has been explained.
Now let sound itself first be discussed.
That object which is apprehended by the ear is sound.
Since the word 'object' is not conventionally used for universals and the like, the word 'object' is included so that soundness should not belong to the word 'sound' itself.
Because it has a common form, there is doubt whether sound is substance or something else, such as quality or action.
He states this:

children.text: pṛthivītvaṃ sajātīyāt salilādeḥ pṛthivyā viśeṣo dṛṣṭaḥ asajātīyābhyāṃ ca guṇakarmabhyām ||
children.translated_text: Earthness is seen as the distinction of earth from things of the same class, such as water, and also from things of a different class, namely quality and action.

children.text: tataḥ śabde'pi kimayaṃ śrotragrāhyatvaṃ viśeṣo guṇaistulyasyārthāntarabhūtasya veti saṃśayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Therefore in the case of sound too there is doubt: is audibility its distinguishing feature while it is similar to qualities, or is it something different from them?
This is not so.

children.text: ekasmin dravye ākāśe vartamānatvānna dravyamayaṃ śabdaḥ dravyaṃ hyadravyaṃ paramāṇvādi anekadravyaṃ vā ghaṭādi ||
children.translated_text: Because it exists in one substance, ether, this sound is not a substance. For a substance is either a non-composite substance, such as an atom, or a substance composed of many substances, such as a pot.

children.text: dravyaṃ karma vā yadindriyāntarapratyakṣaṃ taccākṣuṣamapi dṛṣṭam ayaṃ tu śabdaḥ śrotrapratyakṣo'pi sanna cākṣuṣaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Whatever is a substance or an action and is perceptible by another sense has also been seen to be visible; but this sound, although perceptible by the ear, is not visible.
Thus it is established as a quality.
However:

children.text: karmabhirasya punarguṇabhūtasyāpi sādharmyamapavargo vināśaḥ utpattyanantaramagrahaṇād vināśo'numīyate ||
children.translated_text: It has similarity with actions, even though it is a quality, namely cessation, destruction. Since it is not apprehended immediately after production, its destruction is inferred.
If it is said, 'Even though it exists, it is not apprehended because of some cause,' no.

children.text: yat sadapi nimittānna gṛhyate tasya liṅgaṃ sadbhāvagrāhakaṃ bhavati śabdasya tūccāraṇādūrdhvaṃ saṃyogyāder liṅgasyābhāvādasattaiva ||
children.translated_text: For something that exists but is not apprehended because of a cause has a mark that makes its existence known. But after the utterance of sound, because there is no mark such as conjunction and the like, there is simply non-existence.
Moreover:
The destruction after utterance is a dissimilarity from eternal things; therefore sound is impermanent.
Moreover:
Sound is also an effect, because it is produced from conjunction and the like.
Therefore it is impermanent.
Moreover:
The meaning is: because of prior non-existence.
Because what possesses prior non-existence is destroyed.
And its prior non-existence is known from its production from causes.
Nor are those causes merely manifestors. Why?

children.text: yasmād bheryādikāraṇebhyaḥ śabdasya vikāro'vagamyate mahati bheryādau mahān alpe'lpaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Because a modification of sound is observed from causes such as a drum: when the drum and the like are large, the sound is great; when small, it is small.
But if it were only manifestation:

children.text: nityatvenābhivyaktau śabdo'nyena yajñe prayukto nānyena prayujyeta darbhādivad yātayāmatvādidoṣāt ||
children.translated_text: If sound, being eternal, were merely manifested, then a sound used by one person in a sacrifice could not be used by another, because of faults such as becoming used up, as with darbha grass and the like.
Therefore it is impermanent.
He states why it is an effect:

children.text: bherīdaṇḍasaṃyogād vastradalavibhāgācchabdācca śabdasya vīcisantānavanniṣpatter manyāmahe kāryaḥ śabda iti ||
children.translated_text: We consider sound to be an effect, because sound is produced from the conjunction of drum and stick, from the separation of the halves of cloth, and from another sound, like a continuous series of waves.

children.text: tebhyastrayo vedā ajāyanta iti vacanād vaidikālliṅgād anityaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Because of the Vedic indication in the statement, 'From them the three Vedas were born,' it is impermanent.
Objection: sound is eternal.

children.text: kāryāṇāṃ hi bhāvānāṃ dve pravṛttī ekā nirvṛttiḥ anyā kāryaviniyogarūpā ||
children.translated_text: For produced entities have two activities: one is their coming into being, and the other has the form of being employed as an effect.

children.text: śabdasya punar arthapratipattyarthaiva pravṛttiruccāraṇākhyā nātmārthā tasmānnityaḥ ||
children.translated_text: But sound has only the activity called utterance, for the sake of understanding meaning, and not for its own sake; therefore it is eternal.

children.text: uccaritapradhvaṃsitve śabdasya dvir ayamāmnātaḥ iti vinaṣṭatvāt saṃkhyābhyāvṛttirna bhavet asti ca tasmānnityaḥ ||
children.translated_text: If sound were destroyed after utterance, then in the phrase 'this is recited twice,' since it would have been destroyed, there could be no repetition by number. But there is such repetition; therefore it is eternal.

children.text: prathamāśabdāditi triḥ prathamām anvāha iti vākyam uccaritavināśitve śabdasya prathamāyā ṛco'bhyāvṛttigaṇanaṃ na syāt asti ca tasmānnityaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The sentence 'Because of the word prathamā' or 'he recites the prathamā three times' would not allow counting the repetition of the first ṛc if sound perished when uttered. But such counting exists; therefore it is eternal.

children.text: vināśitve śabdasya sa evāyaṃ gośabdaḥ iti sampratipattiḥ pratyabhijñā na syāt tasmānnityaḥ ||
children.translated_text: If sound were destructible, there could be no shared recognition, the recognition 'this is that very word go.' Therefore it is eternal.
This is not sound.

children.text: pradīpādāv advipravṛttatvaṃ dṛṣṭam dvir vidyunniḥsṛteti saṃkhyābhāvaḥ sampratipattirjvālādau ||
children.translated_text: In lamps and the like, occurrence more than once is observed; in 'lightning has flashed twice' there is number; and in a flame and the like there is shared recognition.
Therefore, because these reasons occur even among impermanent things, all these reasons are doubtful.
Therefore sound is impermanent.
The word prathamā and the existence of shared recognition should be understood in this way, on the basis of similarity.
Since sound and the rest are established as having the nature of qualities and so forth, and since the senses are inferred from them,
therefore now:

children.text: grāhyāṇāmarthānāṃ śabdādīnāṃ yeyaṃ prasiddhiḥ tayā ca śrotrādīnāṃ karaṇānām anayā indriyārthaprasiddhyā ebhyo grāhyagrahaṇebhya indriyārthebhyaḥ paro grahītā ātmā anumīyate ||
children.translated_text: By the established knowledge of the apprehensible objects, sound and the rest, and by the established knowledge of the instruments, hearing and the rest, the self, as a grasper beyond these sense-objects that are apprehended and instruments of apprehension, is inferred.

children.text: grāhyagrahaṇaprasiddhyākhyo grahītṛsadbhāve yo heturuktaḥ so'napadeśaḥ akāraṇamityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The reason called the established knowledge of what is apprehended and of apprehension, which was stated for the existence of a grasper, is anapadeśa, that is, no reason.

children.text: kimātmakalpanayā kathamindriyāṇi grahītṝṇyeva na bhavanti naitat ||
children.translated_text: What need is there to posit a self? Why should the senses themselves not be the graspers? This is not so.
Because the elements, which are the causes of the senses, are unconscious, the senses too, as their effects, are unconscious.
The unconsciousness of the elements:
Because another effect of the elements, such as a pot, is unconscious, the elements too are unconscious.
This sūtra is meant to conclude that, because the elements are unconscious, the senses too are unconscious.

children.text: anyo hetulakṣaṇabāhya ityarthaḥ tathāhi indriyārthaprasiddhir indriyārthadharmatvād ātmanā asaṃbandhānna tamanumāpayet ato'napadeśaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'Another' means outside the definition of a reason. For thus, since the established knowledge of sense-objects is a property of the senses and their objects and has no relation to the self, it would not make that self inferred; therefore it is anapadeśa.
This is not so.
Smoke is conjunct with fire.
A horn inheres in a cow.

children.text: ekārthasamavāyi dvidhā kāryaṃ kāryāntarasya yathā rūpaṃ sparśasya kāraṇaṃ kāraṇāntarasya yathā pāṇiḥ pādasya ||
children.translated_text: What inheres in one and the same thing is of two kinds: an effect is the sign of another effect, as color is of touch; and a cause is the sign of another cause, as a hand is of a foot.

children.text: caturdhā virodhi abhūtaṃ varṣakarma vāyvabhrasaṃyogasya bhūtasya liṅgam bhūtaṃ varṣakarma vāyvabhrasaṃyogasyābhūtasya liṅgam abhūtā śyāmatā abhūtasyāgnisaṃyogasya liṅgam bhūtaṃ kāryaṃ bhūtasya kāraṇasaṃyogasya liṅgam ||
children.translated_text: An opposed sign is fourfold: a future act of rain is a sign of a past conjunction of wind and cloud; a past act of rain is a sign of a future conjunction of wind and cloud; a future blackness is a sign of a future conjunction with fire; and a past effect is a sign of a past conjunction with its cause.

children.text: tasmādiha prasiddhānām indriyārthānāṃ karaṇatā karmatā ca samavāyinī ātmaliṅgam ||
children.translated_text: Therefore here the instrumentality and objecthood of the established senses and sense-objects, as inhering in them, are signs of the self.

children.text: na te ātmani samavāyinī iti cet evametat anyathā tu prayogaḥ indriyāṇi kartṛprayojyāni karaṇatvād vāsyādivaditi ||
children.translated_text: If it is said that they do not inhere in the self, so it is; but the application is otherwise: the senses are set in motion by an agent, because they are instruments, like an axe and the like.
He states how conjunction and the rest are signs:

children.text: prasiddho yaḥ saṃyogyādir nāsaṃbaddho yena saha jñātaḥ sa tasyārthāntarasyāpi liṅgaṃ sambaddhatvāt nāsaṃbaddham ||
children.translated_text: A known thing such as what is conjunct is not unrelated to that with which it is known; because it is related, it is also a sign of that other object, but not if it is unrelated.
Thus:

children.text: aprasiddho viruddhaḥ yasya sādhyadharmeṇa saha naivāsti sambandhaḥ api tu viparyayeṇa asāvanapadeśo 'hetuḥ ||
children.translated_text: An unknown opposed reason, which has no relation at all with the property to be proved but rather with its opposite, is anapadeśa, a non-reason.

children.text: asan yaḥ pakṣe nāsti tenārthādasan asiddha ityarthaḥ saṃdigdhaścānapadeśaḥ saṃdigdho 'naikāntika ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: What is absent, that is, absent from the subject, is in that sense absent, meaning unproved; and the doubtful too is anapadeśa, meaning that the doubtful is inconclusive.
He gives examples:

children.text: ayaṃ padārtho'śvaḥ iti sādhye viṣāṇitvaṃ viruddham aśvaviparyayeṇa viṣāṇitvasya vyāpteḥ ||
children.translated_text: When the thesis is 'this object is a horse,' having horns is opposed, because hornedness is pervaded by the opposite of horse.

children.text: ayaṃ padārtho gauḥ iti sādhye viṣāṇitvam anaikāntikam sādhyaviparyayābhyāṃ vyāptatvāt ||
children.translated_text: When the thesis is 'this object is a cow,' having horns is inconclusive, because it is pervaded by both what is to be proved and its opposite.

children.text: caśabdo'nuktasamuccayārthaḥ śaśo viṣāṇī iti sādhye'siddhaṃ viṣāṇitvam pakṣe'vartamānatvāt ||
children.translated_text: The word 'and' is for the inclusion of what has not been stated: when the thesis is 'a hare has horns,' hornedness is unproved, because it does not occur in the subject.
This has been said incidentally.
Moreover:

children.text: catuṣṭayasannikarṣād yadutpadyate jñānākhyaṃ kāryaṃ tad anyaddhetvantaram ātmajñāpakamastīti ||
children.translated_text: The further cause, which makes known the self, is that other effect called cognition which arises from the conjunction of the four.
Cognition depends on an inherent cause, because it is an effect, like a pot.
The body is meant by the phrase "the inner self."
Activity and cessation of activity, observed in the body, make one infer the self.
The body is presided over by something possessed of effort, because it has activity and cessation from what is beneficial and harmful, like a pot.

children.text: ātmendriyārthānāṃ sannikarṣe yadabhāvājjñānaṃ na bhavati yadbhāve ca bhavati tanmanaḥ ||
children.translated_text: That in whose absence cognition does not arise, and in whose presence it does arise, when self, senses, and objects are in conjunction, is the mind.
Thus the arising and non-arising of cognition are the mark of the mind.
Its qualities are number, magnitude, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and disposition.

children.text: yathā adravyavattvāt paramāṇuvāyordravyatvaṃ nityatvaṃ ca evaṃ manasaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Just as substantiality and eternality belong to atoms and air because they do not possess another substance, so too they belong to the mind.

children.text: bahuṣu kāryeṣu jñeyeṣu ca yugapat prayatnā jñānāni vā na prādurbhavantītyataḥ prayatnajñānāyaugapadyādekaṃ manaḥ pratiśarīraṃ mūrtamasparśaṃ niravayavaṃ nityamaṇu āśucārīti ||
children.translated_text: Since efforts or cognitions do not appear simultaneously with regard to many actions and many objects to be known, because of the non-simultaneity of effort and cognition there is one mind for each body; it is embodied, without touch, partless, eternal, atomic, and swift-moving.

children.text: prāṇāpānanimeṣonmeṣā manogatiśca prayatnakāryatvādātmano liṅgam jīvanamadṛṣṭakāryatvāt indriyāntaravikārāḥ smṛtiprabhavatvāt sukhādayo guṇatvāt ||
children.translated_text: Breathing out and in, closing and opening the eyes, and the movement of the mind are marks of the self because they are effects of effort; life is so because it is an effect of the unseen; transformations of another sense are so because they arise from memory; pleasures and the like are so because they are qualities.

children.text: tiryakpavanasya vāyor dehasthitasya yat prāṇāpānakarma tatprayatnakāryam śarīraparigṛhītavāyuviṣayatve sati vikṛtatvāt bhastrāparigṛhītavāyukarmavat ||
children.translated_text: The action of exhalation and inhalation belonging to the transverse wind, the air situated in the body, is an effect of effort, because, while its object is air contained in a body, it is modified, like the action of air contained in a bellows.

The action of closing and opening the eyes is also an effect of effort, because it is denoted by the words "the action of closing and opening the eyes," like the closing-and-opening action of a wooden machine.

children.text: manasā saṃyoga ātmano 'dṛṣṭāpekṣo jīvanam śarīravṛddhyādi tatkāryam api jīvanam śarīraṃ prayatnavatādhiṣṭhitaṃ vṛddhikṣatabhagnasaṃrohaṇanimittatvāt jīrṇagṛhavat ||
children.translated_text: Life is the conjunction of the self with the mind, dependent on the unseen; growth and the like of the body are also its effects. The living body is presided over by something possessed of effort, because it is the cause of growth and the healing of cuts and breaks, like an old house.

children.text: indriyāntaraṃ prati manaso gamanaṃ manogatiḥ prayatnakāryā abhimatapradeśasambandhanimittatvāt pelakakriyāvat sā hi dārakaprayatnakṛtā ||
children.translated_text: The mind's going toward another sense is movement of the mind; it is an effect of effort, because it is the cause of connection with the intended place, like the motion of a ball; for that is produced by a child's effort.

children.text: rūpālocanasaṃskāravyaktirasasmaraṇaprayatnamanaḥkriyārasanamanaḥsambandharasanavikārāṇāṃ pūrvasya pūrvasya kāraṇatvādutpattiḥ jñaptis tu vaiparītyena uttarottarasmāt pūrvasya pūrvasya smaraṇena ātmā anumīyate ||
children.translated_text: The manifestation of the disposition from seeing a form, the effort of remembering a taste, the action of the mind, the connection of the tongue with the mind, and the transformation of the tongue arise because each preceding item is the cause of the next. But cognition proceeds in the reverse direction: from each later item, through memory of the preceding one, the self is inferred.
Memory does not belong to the senses, since when one thing has been seen by one sense, another sense would have memory of that object.
Nor does it belong to a part of the body, because that differs according to its condition.

children.text: devadattasya rūparasagandhasparśapratyayā ekānekanimittāḥ mayā iti pratyayena pratisaṃdhānāt kṛtasaṃketānāṃ bahūnāmekasmin nartakībhrūkṣepe yugapadanekapratyayavat iti uddyotakaraḥ ||
children.translated_text: According to <s>Uddyotakara</s>, <s>Devadatta</s>'s cognitions of form, taste, smell, and touch have one and many causes, because they are connected by the cognition "by me," like the simultaneous many cognitions of many people who know a convention when a dancer moves her eyebrow at one place.
Pleasure and the like depend on something possessing qualities, because they are qualities, like color.
Because they do not possess another substance, substantiality and eternality belong to them as to atoms and air.
But, one may object:

children.text: yathā cākṣuṣārthasannikarṣe sati yajñadatto 'yam iti pratyakṣaṃ bhavati na tathā prāṇādisukhādisambaddho 'yamātmeti jñānaṃ jāyate ||
children.translated_text: When there is contact with an object of sight, a perception arises, "This is <s>Yajñadatta</s>." But no such cognition arises, "This is the self connected with breath and pleasure and the like."

children.text: atha kathamadṛṣṭasambandhaṃ prāṇādi ātmano liṅgam tadāha na prāṇādi dṛṣṭaṃ liṅgam ||
children.translated_text: Then how can breath and the rest, whose connection is not perceived, be a mark of the self? He replies: breath and the rest are not a perceived mark.

children.text: prāṇādīnāṃ nirnimittānāṃ sukhādīnāṃ cānāśritānāmanutpattiḥ ata eṣāṃ kenāpi nimittenāśrayeṇa bhāvyam ityato'pi sāmānyatodṛṣṭād ākāśādīnām anirāsād aviśeṣaḥ teṣāmapi hetutvasambhavāt ||
children.translated_text: Breath and the rest, if without a cause, and pleasure and the rest, if without a substratum, would not arise; therefore they must have some cause and substratum. Yet because ether and the others are not excluded by this generally observed inference, there is no specificity, since they too could be causes.
The meaning is that "the self exists" would be merely common talk.
This is not so.

children.text: ahamiti śabdena kṣityādibhinnātmadravyaviṣayeṇa aikādhikaraṇyāt ahaṃ prāṇādimān ahaṃ sukhavān iti ||
children.translated_text: For the word "I" has the same locus as a self-substance distinct from earth and the other elements, as in "I have breath and the rest" and "I have pleasure."
Therefore it is not merely scriptural testimony, because breath and the rest are marks.
But, one may object:

children.text: yadi khalvahaṃ devadatto'haṃ yajñadatta ityātmani dṛṣṭapratyakṣamidaṃ bhavet evaṃ yujyeta ahaṃśabdasyātmavācakatvam yāvatā śarīrābhidhāyakadevadattaśabdaikārthādhikaraṇatvād ahaṃśabdo'pi śarīravācakaḥ ||
children.translated_text: If this direct perception with respect to the self, "I am <s>Devadatta</s>," "I am <s>Yajñadatta</s>," were in fact seen, then the word "I" could properly denote the self. But since it has the same referent as the word <s>Devadatta</s>, which denotes the body, the word "I" too denotes the body.
Therefore breath, pleasure, and the like are not causes for determining the self.
How is the word <s>Devadatta</s> applied to the body? He explains:

children.text: gamanavācinā gacchati iti śabdena saha prayogād devadattaśabdaḥ śarīravacano 'vasīyate ātmano gatyasambhavāt ||
children.translated_text: Because it is used together with the word "goes," which denotes motion, the word <s>Devadatta</s> is ascertained to denote the body, since motion is impossible for the self.

children.text: tasmād ahaṃśabdo'pi śarīre eva devadattaśabdena saha dṛṣṭatvāt ||
children.translated_text: Therefore the word "I" too applies only to the body, because it is observed together with the word <s>Devadatta</s>.
This is not so.

children.text: devadattaśabdena ekārthādhikaraṇatvād yo'yamupacāro 'haṃśabdasya śarīre sa saṃdigdhaḥ kiṃ śarīrasya ātmopakārakatvād ahaṃśabda ātmābhidhāyaka upacarita uta mukhyatayā śarīrasyābhidhāyakaḥ iti na śarīrātmanor ahaṃśabdasya niścayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Because it has the same referent as the word <s>Devadatta</s>, the figurative use of the word "I" for the body is doubtful: is the word "I," while denoting the self, figuratively applied because the body serves the self, or does it primarily denote the body? Thus there is no certainty that the word "I" applies to either the body or the self.
He states the certainty in his own position:
In the phrase "in the inner self," it means the self; in the phrase "in what is other," it means the body.

children.text: yadi ahaṃśabdaḥ śarīravacanaḥ syāt evaṃ sati tasmin piṇḍe devadattaśabda iva sarvaiḥ prayujyeta ||
children.translated_text: If the word "I" denoted the body, then, this being so, it would be used by everyone for that mass, just like the word <s>Devadatta</s>.
But not so in this way; therefore it is in the self, which is another entity.
The word 'I' is directly evident.

children.text: śarīra iva ātmanyapi parairaprayogānna syāditi cet ata āha ||
children.translated_text: If it is objected that, just as in the case of the body, it would not apply to the self either, because others do not use it, he therefore says:

children.text: yajñadattaviṣṇumitrayoḥ sambandhinaḥ śarīraviśeṣād yathā dṛṣṭānna tadīye sukhādāvasmadādīnāṃ jāyate jñānaṃ tathaiva na tadīyāhaṅkāro 'smābhiḥ saṃvedyate yato'haṃśabdaḥ prayujyeta ||
children.translated_text: Just as, from seeing the particular body connected with <s>Yajñadatta</s> or <s>Viṣṇumitra</s>, knowledge does not arise in us concerning his pleasure and the like, so too his ego-cognition is not experienced by us, and therefore the word 'I' would not be used.

children.text: śarīravācakatve tu yathā śarīraṃ dṛṣṭvā tatra devadattaśabdaṃ prayuñjate tadvadimamapi prayuñjīran na tvevam ||
children.translated_text: But if it denoted the body, then just as, on seeing the body there, people use the word <s>Devadatta</s>, so they would also use this word; but it is not so.
Therefore it is not in the body.
But if it resides in the self, non-use by others is accounted for.

children.text: evamahaṃśabdena ekādhikaraṇatvāt sukhādaya ātmaviṣayāḥ prāṇādayaśca tannimittāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus, because they have the same substratum as the word 'I,' pleasure and the rest have the self as their object, and the breaths and the rest have that as their cause.
Objection:

children.text: yathā salliṅgāviśeṣād viśeṣaliṅgābhāvāccaiko bhāvas tathaiva sukhaduḥkhajñānānāṃ niṣpattyaviśeṣād viśeṣaliṅgābhāvāccaikātmyam ||
children.translated_text: Just as, because there is no distinction in the mark of being and because there is no special mark, being is one, so too, because there is no distinction in the production of pleasures, pains, and cognitions, and because there is no special mark, there is one self.
This is not so.

children.text: anyasya sukhādiyoge'nyasya tadabhāvādanayā vyavasthayā nānā ātmānaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Since pleasure and the like are connected with one person and absent in another, by this arrangement selves are many.

children.text: grāmakāmo yajeta svargakāmo yajeta ityato'pi śāstrasāmarthyān nānā ātmānaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Also from the force of scripture, as in 'one who desires a village should sacrifice' and 'one who desires heaven should sacrifice,' selves are many.
Its distinctive Vaiśeṣika qualities are cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, unseen potency, and disposition.
But the others are number, magnitude, separateness, conjunction, and disjunction.

children.text: adravyavattvādityanena yat sat kāraṇarahitaṃ tan nityamuktaṃ paramāṇvādi ||
children.translated_text: By the statement 'because it does not possess another substance,' whatever exists without a cause is eternally free, such as atoms and the like.
But with respect to apprehension:

children.text: tasya paramāṇvāder indriyair agṛhyamāṇasyāpi śarīramahābhūtādi kāryaṃ liṅgam ||
children.translated_text: For that atom and the like, although not grasped by the senses, an effect such as a body or the great elements is the mark.

children.text: yasmāt kāraṇebhyastantvādibhyaḥ paṭādi kāryamutpadyate'taḥ kāryasya kāraṇapūrvakatvāt kāraṇasya kāryaṃ liṅgam ||
children.translated_text: Since an effect such as cloth arises from causes such as threads, therefore, because an effect is preceded by a cause, the effect is the mark of the cause.

children.text: yadā khalu sarvaṃ kāryamanityam ityucyate tadānena nityatvasya viśeṣapratiṣedhena kāryaviṣayeṇa kiṃcit kāraṇaṃ nityamiti jñāyate ||
children.translated_text: When it is said that every effect is impermanent, then by this specific denial of eternality with regard to effects it is understood that some cause is eternal.

children.text: avidyā agrahaṇamatīndriyatvena paramāṇūnām tadapi anityatvaṃ nivārayati ||
children.translated_text: Non-apprehension, because the atoms are beyond the senses, also rules out their impermanence.

children.text: adṛśyamāne hyarthe tadgatam anityatvaṃ kena gṛhyeta ||
children.translated_text: For when an object is not being seen, by what could impermanence belonging to it be grasped?
Therefore impermanence cannot be asserted.
If it is asked, how is apprehension possible?

children.text: mahattvaparimāṇasamavāyini dravye samavāyikāraṇadravyabahutvād rūpācca śuklāderjñānaṃ bhavati kuta etat yataḥ ||
children.translated_text: In a substance in which the measure of largeness inheres, cognition of white and other colors arises because of the multiplicity of substances that are its inherent causes and because of color. Whence is this known? Because:
Even though color exists in an atom, there is no apprehension, because the atom lacks substances that are its inherent causes.

children.text: satyapi anekadravyavattve mahattve ca rūpākhyasya saṃskārasyābhāvād vāyāvanupalabdhiḥ ||
children.translated_text: And even though air possesses many substances and largeness, there is no apprehension, because the disposition called color is absent.
Since a qualified multiplicity of substances is grasped, non-apprehension is established even in a triad.
How is it in the case of color?

children.text: mahatā anekadravyasamavāyidravyeṇa ghaṭādinā rūpaguṇasya samavāyād rūpaviśeṣācca rūpatvākhyāt sāmānyaviśeṣād upalabdhiḥ ||
children.translated_text: There is apprehension because the quality color inheres in a large substance composed of many substances, such as a pot, and because of the particular form of color, namely the general-specific property called colorhood.

children.text: etena anantaroktena nyāyena anekadravyeṇa dravyeṇa samavāyād rasatvādisāmānyaviśeṣebhyaśca rasādīnāmupalabdhiḥ ||
children.translated_text: By this same reasoning just stated, tastes and the rest are apprehended because they inhere in a substance composed of many substances and because of the general-specific properties such as tastehood and the like.

children.text: paramāṇurūpasyānekadravyeṇa dravyeṇa samavāyābhāvānnopalabdhiḥ tato'nekadravyeṇa dravyeṇa samavāyasya rūpopalabdheścāvyabhicāraḥ ||
children.translated_text: The color of an atom is not apprehended because it does not inhere in a substance composed of many substances; therefore inherence in a substance composed of many substances is invariably connected with the apprehension of color.

children.text: rūpīti viśiṣṭaṃ rūpi tena upalabdhiyogyena rūpiṇā samavāyādetāni cākṣuṣāṇi svasāmānyaviśeṣebhyaśca ||
children.translated_text: 'Colored' means qualified by color; because these inhere in a colored thing fit for apprehension, and because of their own general-specific properties, they are visible to the eye.
Why?

children.text: yasmād rūparahiteṣu mahatsu dravyāntareṣu sthitāni na jñāyante ||
children.translated_text: Because when they are situated in other large substances that are devoid of color, they are not known.

children.text: yathaiva mahatyanekadravyeṇa samavāyād rūpādīnāṃ samavetānāmupalabdhirevaṃ mahati samaveteṣu guṇeṣu samavetayor guṇatvabhāvayos tais tair guṇai rūpādibhiḥ samavāyād yathāsvaṃ cakṣurādīndriyair upalabdhiḥ na tu sāmānyaviśeṣās teṣūpalambhakās tadabhāvāt ||
children.translated_text: Just as colors and the rest that inhere in something large are apprehended because of inherence in a substance composed of many substances, so the qualityhood and existence that inhere in qualities inhering in something large are apprehended by their respective senses, such as the eye, through inherence with those particular qualities such as color and the rest; but the general-specific properties are not apprehenders in them, because these are absent.

children.text: evaṃ tattvādīnāṃ svairindriyaiḥ dravye tu bhāvasya samavāyāt ||
children.translated_text: In the same way, substancehood and the rest are apprehended by their own senses; but in the case of substance, existence is apprehended because of inherence.
In action, it is through inherence in what inheres, as in the case of qualities.

children.text: kṣityādipañcakena śarīrārambhe trayāṇāṃ pratyakṣatvād vāyorapratyakṣatvād yathā tadvatā saṃyogo'pyapratyakṣa evaṃ śarīramapratyakṣaṃ syāt pratyakṣāpratyakṣair ārabdhatvāt ||
children.translated_text: If the body were begun by the five, earth and the rest, then, since three are perceptible and air is imperceptible, just as conjunction with that is imperceptible, so the body too would be imperceptible, because it would be begun by both perceptible and imperceptible things.
But because it is perceptible, we think that it is not begun by the five.
Objection: then it could be begun by the three perceptible elements.

children.text: kṣitisalilānalair ārambhe vilakṣaṇebhyo rūpādibhyaḥ kārye vilakṣaṇāni rūpāṇi guṇāntarāṇi jāyeran ||
children.translated_text: If it were begun by earth, water, and fire, then from distinct colors and the like, distinct colors, other qualities, would arise in the effect.
But it is not so.
Rather, we apprehend only earthy colors and the like.
Therefore it is not threefold in nature.

children.text: ātmaśabdena svarūpam svarūpeṇa pañcānāmapi bhūtānāṃ parasparasaṃyogo na pratiṣidhyate śarīre 'nārambhakatvena ||
children.translated_text: By the word 'nature' its own form is meant; mutual conjunction of all five elements according to their own forms is not denied in the body, but they are denied as originators.
In an earthy body, water and the others are conjoined, not inhering causes.
Only a womb-born body is begun by water and the others, as in the world of <s>Varuṇa</s> and so on.
Why?

children.text: anekadeśāḥ paramāṇavaḥ tairevārabhyate jalādiśarīram na śukraśoṇitābhyām ||
children.translated_text: Atoms belong to many regions; by those very atoms the bodies of water and the like are begun, not by semen and blood.
And this is so:

children.text: dharmaviśeṣāpekṣāḥ paramāṇava eva śarīramārabhante na śukrādi ||
children.translated_text: Atoms, dependent on a particular <s>dharma</s> (merit), alone begin the body, not semen and the rest.

children.text: kathaṃ hi puṇyavatāṃ śukrādimayaṃ śarīraṃ syāt ||
children.translated_text: For how could the body of meritorious beings consist of semen and the like?
And for this further reason:
From the particular effect called the bodies of locusts and the like, we think that there are non-womb-born beings.
And for this further reason:
Because of designations such as '<s>Aṅgiras</s>, born from coals,' and the like, we think that there are non-womb-born beings.

children.text: yataḥ pratyakṣeṇa aṅgārajanmādikam arthaṃ dṛṣṭvā puruṣaiḥ praṇīyante saṃjñāḥ ||
children.translated_text: For after seeing by perception such a fact as birth from coals, people institute names.
Such as '<s>Aṅgiras</s>' and the like.
Therefore, since names have a beginning, the designation is according to fact.
Therefore:

children.text: candramā manaso jātaḥ ityādikācca vedaliṅgāt santyayonijāḥ śarīraviśeṣāḥ ||
children.translated_text: And from a Vedic indication such as 'the moon was born from the mind,' there are particular bodies that are non-womb-born.
Thus a body of water and the like is precisely non-womb-born.
But an earthy body is both womb-born and non-womb-born.

children.text: svāśrayasaṃyogāpekṣitvāt prayatnasya kriyārambhe ātmahastasaṃyogaḥ karmaṇaḥ kāraṇam ||
children.translated_text: Because effort depends on conjunction with its own substratum at the beginning of an action, conjunction of the self with the hand is a cause of the action.
Because conjunction is a cause that depends on something further, effort too is a cause.
Therefore action in the hand arises from the two.

children.text: tatheti saṅkhyāmātrātideśaḥ tena hastamusalasaṃyogo musalakarmaṇaḥ kāraṇaṃ pūrvādhikṛtaśca prayatnaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'Likewise' is an extension only with respect to number; by it, the conjunction of hand and pestle is the cause of the pestle's action, and so is the previously mentioned effort.

children.text: na tu ātmahastasaṃyogo'samavāyikāraṇaṃ musalakarmaṇi ātmasaṃyuktahastasaṃyogādeva tatsiddheḥ ||
children.translated_text: But conjunction of self and hand is not the non-inherent cause in the action of the pestle, because that is established just from the conjunction of the hand connected with the self.

children.text: vegavaddravyasaṃyogo'bhighātaḥ ulūkhalābhighātād utpanne musalasyotpatanakarmaṇi akāraṇaṃ hastamusalasaṃyogaḥ pūrvaprayatnasyābhighātād vinaṣṭatvāt utpatatu musaladravyam itīcchāyā abhāvāt prayatnāntarasyābhāvaḥ saṃyogasya ca guṇakarmārambhe sāpekṣakāraṇatvāt prayatnarahito hastamusalasaṃyogo na kāraṇamutpatanasya ||
children.translated_text: Impact is conjunction with a substance possessing velocity. In the upward action of the pestle produced by impact with the mortar, the conjunction of hand and pestle is not a cause: since the previous effort has been destroyed by the impact, and since there is no desire, 'let the pestle substance fly upward,' there is no further effort. And because conjunction is a dependent cause in the production of qualities and actions, the hand-pestle conjunction, being without effort, is not the cause of the upward motion.

children.text: yathaiva hastamusalasaṃyogo musalotpatanakarmaṇi na kāraṇaṃ tathātmahastasaṃyogo'pi hastotpatanakarmaṇi na kāraṇaṃ saṃyogasya sāpekṣakāraṇatvāt ||
children.translated_text: Just as the hand-pestle conjunction is not the cause in the pestle's upward action, so too the self-hand conjunction is not the cause in the hand's upward action, because conjunction is a dependent cause.

children.text: musalena sahotpatatu hastaḥ iti abhisaṃdher abhāvena prayatnasya cābhāvāt ||
children.translated_text: For there is no intention, 'let the hand fly up together with the pestle,' and there is no effort.
If it is asked, 'Whence, then, is the upward motion of the two?'
The impact of the mortar is the cause of the pestle's upward action.
But the hand-pestle conjunction, dependent on the velocity residing in the pestle, is the cause of the action of the hand; the impact is not, because it does not inhere there.

children.text: ātmeti śarīraikadeśaḥ yathā caitadapratyayaṃ haste musale ca karma tathaiva hastāvayavasaṃyogāddhastagatavegāpekṣād hastotpatanakāle'vayave tasminnapratyayaṃ karma jāyate ||
children.translated_text: 'Self' here means a part of the body. And just as this action in the hand and pestle is without cognition, so too, at the time when the hand flies upward, an action without cognition arises in that bodily part from conjunction with the parts of the hand, dependent on the velocity residing in the hand.
When the hand-pestle conjunction has ceased through disjunction, falling occurs because of heaviness.

children.text: nudyate 'neneti nodanaṃ vegaprayatnāpekṣaḥ saṃyogaviśeṣaḥ prerakaprayatnābhāve nodanābhāvān nordhvaṃ tiryag vā kevalād gurutvān musalādergamanakarma bhavati ||
children.translated_text: That by which something is impelled is called <s>nodana</s> (propulsion): it is a particular conjunction dependent on velocity and effort. Since there is no propulsion when the impelling effort is absent, the motion of a pestle and the like upward or sideways does not occur from gravity alone.
Whence comes a particular propulsion?

children.text: atra idaṃ kṣipāmi iti icchāviśeṣajaḥ prayatna utpanno hastāderdravyasya dravyāntareṇa saṃyogaṃ nodanākhyaṃ janayati ||
children.translated_text: Here, an effort produced by the particular desire 'I throw this' generates in the hand and the like a conjunction with another substance called propulsion.
A particular propulsion born from effort qualified by the desire to send something to a distant place effects the throwing to a distant place.

children.text: yad garbhasya spandanādikarma tadātmaśarīraikadeśasaṃyogāj jīvanapūrvakaprayatnāpekṣād bhavatīti sapratyayam mātuḥ kāryāvaskaropasarpaṇakarma garbhasyāpratyayamātmasaṃyogādadṛṣṭāpekṣād bhavatīti ||
children.translated_text: The motion such as stirring of an embryo occurs from the conjunction of self and a part of the body, dependent on effort preceded by life, and is therefore accompanied by cognition; the mother's approach toward the refuse connected with her work occurs without cognition on the embryo's part, from conjunction with the self dependent on unseen potency.

children.text: vyāsakte manasi yad dagdhasya hastāder vikṣepaṇaṃ tadapi jīvanapūrvakaprayatnāpekṣād ātmahastasaṃyogād bhavatīti nāpratyayam ||
children.translated_text: When the mind is occupied elsewhere, the casting away of a burned hand or the like also occurs from self-hand conjunction dependent on effort preceded by life; therefore it is not without cognition.

children.text: śarīravidhārakaprayatnābhāve suptasyāṅgānāṃ patanaṃ gurutvād bhavati tadābhisaṃdher abhāvāt ||
children.translated_text: When there is no effort maintaining the body, the falling of the limbs of a sleeping person occurs because of heaviness, since at that time there is no intention.

children.text: vegāpekṣād vāyutṛṇasaṃyogāt tṛṇādīnāṃ karma teṣāṃ prayatnābhāvāt ||
children.translated_text: The action of grass and the like comes from conjunction of wind and grass dependent on velocity, because those things have no effort.

children.text: maṇīnāṃ taskaraṃ prati gamanaṃ sūcīnāṃ cāyaskāntaṃ prati dharmādharmakṛtam ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The movement of jewels toward a thief, and of needles toward a lodestone, is caused by merit and demerit; this is the meaning.

children.text: nodanādādyaṃ karma saṃskārād bahūni karmāṇi iṣāvutpadyante ||
children.translated_text: In an arrow, the first action arises from propulsion, and many actions arise from <s>saṃskāra</s> (residual impulse).

children.text: ekasmiṃstu karmaṇi prathameṇaivākāśasaṃyogena vinaṣṭatvāt karmaṇa uttarasaṃyogavibhāgā notpadyeran tasmādiṣāvanekaṃ karma ||
children.translated_text: But if there were a single action, since that action would be destroyed by the very first conjunction with space, later conjunctions and disjunctions would not arise. Therefore there are many actions in an arrow.

children.text: jyāśarasaṃyogaḥ prayatnāpekṣo jyāgatavegāpekṣo vā nodanam tata ādyam iṣoḥ karma nodanāpekṣaṃ saṃskāraṃ karoti nirapekṣaṃ tu saṃyogavibhāgau ||
children.translated_text: The conjunction of bowstring and arrow, dependent on effort or dependent on the velocity residing in the bowstring, is propulsion. From that, the arrow's first action, dependent on propulsion, produces <s>saṃskāra</s> (residual impulse), while it independently produces conjunction and disjunction.

children.text: tataḥ saṃyogād vinaṣṭe karmaṇi nodane vibhāgād vinivṛtte ādyakarmajasaṃskāra uttaramiṣau karma karoti tathottaramuttaraṃ paunaḥpunyenetyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Then, when the action has been destroyed by conjunction and the propulsion has ceased through disjunction, the <s>saṃskāra</s> produced by the first action produces the next action in the arrow, and in the same way each subsequent one again and again; this is the meaning.
When <s>saṃskāra</s> is destroyed by conjunction with a substance possessing touch, heaviness produces its falling action.

children.text: samastān vyastāṃśca gurutvadravatvavegaprayatnānapekṣamāṇo yaḥ saṃyogaviśeṣo nodanāt preraṇād avibhāgahetoḥ karmaṇaḥ kāraṇaṃ tannodanam tathāhi pādādibhir nudyamānāyāṃ paṅkākhyāyāṃ pṛthivyāṃ karma jāyate ||
children.translated_text: That special conjunction which, without depending on heaviness, fluidity, velocity, or effort, is the cause of an action that brings about disjunction, through pushing or impelling, is called impulse. Thus, when the earth called mud is pushed by feet and the like, motion arises.

children.text: vegāpekṣo'bhighātād abhihanyamānasya vibhāgahetoḥ karmaṇaḥ kāraṇaṃ saṃyogo'bhighātaḥ tathāhi rathādibhirabhighātāt pṛthivyekadeśeṣu dṛśyate karma ||
children.translated_text: Impact is the conjunction, dependent on velocity, which is the cause of an action that brings about disjunction in something being struck by a blow. Thus, from impact by chariots and the like, motion is seen in parts of earth.

children.text: saṃyuktasaṃyogācca nudyamānābhihanyamānābhyāṃ ca saṃyukteṣu bhavanti karmāṇi ||
children.translated_text: And from conjunction with what is conjoined, motions occur in things conjoined with what is being pushed and struck.

children.text: yat khalu viruddhakriyavāyusaṃyogāt sarvasyāṃ pṛthivyāṃ kampādi karma prajānāṃ śubhāśubhasūcanāyotpadyate tat sarveṣāmeva śubhāśubhasūcanād viśeṣeṇādṛṣṭakāritam ||
children.translated_text: That motion, such as trembling, which arises throughout the whole earth from conjunction with winds moving in contrary directions, in order to indicate good and bad fortune for living beings, is especially produced by <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen potency), because it indicates good and bad fortune for all.
When there is no conjunction of water with a supporting wind and cloud, falling motion occurs because of its heaviness.

children.text: sasyānāṃ samṛddhaye vināśāya vā sarvajanānāmadṛṣṭena janitaṃ patanakarma adṛṣṭakāritam ucyate ||
children.translated_text: The falling motion produced by the <s>adṛṣṭa</s> of all people for the prosperity or destruction of crops is said to be produced by <s>adṛṣṭa</s>.
Because of the absence of a support, the flowing motion of water occurs because of fluidity.

children.text: nāḍīti raśmiḥ saviturdvau raśmī śuciśca śukraśca ||
children.translated_text: A tube means a ray of the sun; the two rays are <s>Śuci</s> and <s>Śukra</s>.

children.text: śucir apa ādatte śukreṇa vṛddhiṃ karoti ||
children.translated_text: <s>Śuci</s> takes up the waters, and through <s>Śukra</s> it makes them increase.
Ascent occurs by means of the tube called <s>Śuci</s>, conjoined with wind, in dependence on the effort of the sun.

children.text: nodanāccitradaṇḍādibhirārohaṇam pīḍanād vastrādibhiḥ pīḍyamānanudyamānābhyāṃ ca saṃyukte ||
children.translated_text: Ascent also occurs from impulse, by variegated sticks and the like, and in things conjoined with what is being pressed and pushed, by pressure with cloths and the like.

children.text: vṛkṣamūle niṣiktānām apāṃ vṛkṣopari gamanamadṛṣṭena kriyata iti ||
children.translated_text: The movement upward in a tree of waters poured at the root of the tree is produced by <s>adṛṣṭa</s>; so it is said.

children.text: apāṃ saṅghātaḥ kāṭhinyaṃ divyena tejasā saṃyogāt divyabhaumābhyāṃ tu vilayanam ||
children.translated_text: The aggregation of waters is hardness, owing to conjunction with celestial fire; but melting occurs through both celestial and terrestrial fire.

children.text: asti divyāsu apsu tejaḥ ityatra tejasaḥ avasphūrjathurabhrānniḥsaraṇaṃ liṅgamiti ||
children.translated_text: In the statement that there is fire in celestial waters, the sign of fire is lightning, the issuing forth from a cloud.

children.text: tā agniṃ garbhaṃ dadhire vabhūṣā iti ca vaidikaṃ vākyaṃ divyāsvapsu tejaso liṅgamiti ||
children.translated_text: And the Vedic sentence, “they bore Agni as an embryo, desiring adornment,” is a sign of fire in celestial waters.
The sound of cloud-lightning is thunder.

children.text: viruddhadikkriyābhyāṃ vāyubhyām apāṃ preryamāṇānāṃ taraṅgabhūtānāṃ parasparābhighātākhyāt saṃyogācchabdaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Sound arises from the conjunction called mutual impact of waters that have become waves and are being impelled by two winds whose directions and motions are opposed.

children.text: ekenāpi prakupitena vāyunā vyavacchidyamānānām apāṃ vibhāgācchabdaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Or, even from one raging wind, sound arises from the disjunction of waters being split apart.

children.text: yathā nodanābhighātasaṃyuktasaṃyogādṛṣṭebhyaḥ pṛthivyāṃ karma tathā tejaso vāyośca ||
children.translated_text: Just as motion in earth arises from impulse, impact, conjunction with what is conjoined, and <s>adṛṣṭa</s>, so too motion belongs to fire and air.
This is irregular motion.
But regular motion is as follows.

children.text: agneravasthāne tiryag vā gamane pacyamānasyābhasmībhāvaḥ syād apāṃ vā tathā vāyor atiryaggamane pūyamānadravyāṇāṃ pavanābhāvo 'gneścāprabodhaḥ vinaṣṭaśarīrāṇāmātmanāṃ sargādau pṛthivyādiparamāṇuṣvādyaṃ parasparopasarpaṇakarma na syāt tathā labdhabhūmīnāṃ yogināṃ kalpānte 'bhisaṃdhāya prayatnena manaḥ śarīrād vyatiricyāvatiṣṭhamānānāṃ sargādau navaśarīrasaṃbandhāya manasa ādyaṃ karma na bhavet adṛṣṭādṛte ||
children.translated_text: If, apart from <s>adṛṣṭa</s>, fire remained in place or moved sideways, there would be no reduction to ash of what is being cooked; likewise with water. If air did not move sideways, there would be no blowing upon things being purified, and there would be no kindling of fire. At the beginning of creation, there would be no first motion of mutual approach among earth-atoms and the other atoms for selves whose bodies had perished. Similarly, for yogins who have attained the stages, whose minds at the end of an age remain apart from the body through effort based on resolve, there would be no first motion of the mind at the beginning of creation for connection with a new body.

children.text: tasmādagner ūrdhvajvalanaṃ vāyośca tiryakpavanam aṇūnāṃ copasarpaṇakarma manasaścādyaṃ karma etāni prāṇināmadṛṣṭena kṛtāni ||
children.translated_text: Therefore the upward flaming of fire, the sideways blowing of air, the motion of approach of atoms, and the first motion of the mind: these are produced by the <s>adṛṣṭa</s> of living beings.

children.text: yathātmasaṃyogaprayatnābhyāṃ haste karma tathātmamanaḥsaṃyogāt prayatnācca manasaḥ karma etat sadehasya karma tatra jāgrata icchādveṣapūrvakāt prayatnāt prabodhakāle tu jīvanapūrvakāt ||
children.translated_text: Just as action in the hand arises from conjunction of self and effort, so action of the mind arises from conjunction of self and mind and from effort. This is action of one who has a body: in the waking state it comes from effort preceded by desire and aversion, but at the time of awakening it comes from life.

children.text: yataḥ saṃyogo yogaḥ sa ca karmakāryo'to yogāṅgaṃ karma yogamokṣau ca karmādhikāre'pyucyete ||
children.translated_text: Since conjunction is yoga, and that is produced by action, action is a limb of yoga; and yoga and liberation are also taught in the section on action.

children.text: yato hetorātmendriyamano'rthasannikarṣo jñānakāraṇatvena sukhaduḥkhe janayatyatastadanārambhaḥ tasya sannikarṣasyānārambho'nutpattirucyata iti
children.translated_text: For, because contact among self, sense organ, mind, and object produces pleasure and pain as a cause of cognition, its non-arising, that is, the non-production of that contact, is being taught.
For thus:

children.text: yadā hi ātmani mano'vasthitaṃ nendriyeṣu tadā catuṣṭayasannikarṣasyānārambhāt tatkāryayoḥ sukhaduḥkhayor abhāvarūpo vidyamānaśarīrasyātmano vāyunigrahāpekṣa ātmano manasā saṃyogo yogaḥ ||
children.translated_text: When the mind rests in the self and not in the senses, then, because the fourfold contact does not arise, there is an absence of its effects, pleasure and pain. The conjunction of the self with the mind, in the case of a self whose body still exists and dependent on restraint of breath, is yoga.
Why is the action of breath-control not stated as a limb of yoga?

children.text: iha ātmaśabdena vāyuḥ yathātmasaṃyogaprayatnābhyāṃ haste karma tathātmavāyusaṃyogāt prayatnācca prāṇāyāmakarma ||
children.translated_text: Here, by the word self, air is meant: just as action in the hand arises from conjunction of self and effort, so the action of breath-control arises from conjunction of self and air and from effort.

children.text: maraṇakāle pūrvaśarīrānmanaso niḥsaraṇamapasarpaṇam śarīrāntareṇābhisambandho manasa upasarpaṇam śukraśoṇitāt prabhṛti garbhasthasya mātrā upayuktenānnapānena nāḍyanupraviṣṭena sambandho 'śitapītasaṃyogaḥ kalalārbudamāṃsapeśīghanaśarīrādibhir ekasminneva saṃsāre ye sambandhāste kāryāntarasaṃyogāḥ tānyapasarpaṇādīnyadṛṣṭenaiva kriyante na prayatnena ||
children.translated_text: At the time of death, the mind’s departure from the former body is withdrawal; its connection with another body is the mind’s approach. From semen and blood onward, the relation of the embryo to food and drink consumed by the mother and entered through the channels is conjunction with what has been eaten and drunk. Those relations, within one and the same transmigratory existence, with the drop, the lump, the mass of flesh, the dense body, and so on, are conjunctions with further effects. These, beginning with withdrawal and the rest, are brought about by <s>adṛṣṭa</s> alone, not by effort.

children.text: evaṃrūpasyānādyapasarpaṇādinimittasyādṛṣṭasyābhāve jīvanākhyasyātmamanaḥsaṃyogasyābhāvo 'nyasya ca śarīrasyāprādurbhāvo yaḥ sa mokṣaḥ ||
children.translated_text: When there is absence of <s>adṛṣṭa</s> of this kind, which is beginningless and is the cause of withdrawal and the rest, there is absence of the self-mind conjunction called life, and no other body comes into being; that is liberation.
Because, when all things are covered by darkness, cognition does not arise, darkness is a cause.
Again, that:

children.text: vināśitvena nityair dravyair vaidharmyād amūrtatvāsparśatvaprakāśavirodhair anityadravyair vaidharmyānna dravyaṃ tamaḥ na ca guṇaḥ karma vā āśrayānupalabdheḥ ||
children.translated_text: Because, by being perishable, it differs from the eternal substances, and because, through formlessness, intangibility, and opposition to light, it differs from impermanent substances, darkness is not a substance. Nor is it a quality or an action, because no substratum is apprehended.
Therefore darkness is only the mere absence of light.
Whence is this known?

children.text: tejasaḥ savitṛprakāśāderbahiḥ sadbhāvāt parvataguhādau ca dravyāntareṇāvṛte 'bhāvānmanyāmahe tejaso'bhāvamātraṃ tama iti ||
children.translated_text: Because outside the light of fire, sun, and the like there is the presence of light, while in a mountain cave and so on, when covered by another substance, there is its absence; therefore we think that darkness is merely the absence of light.

children.text: bāhyaṃ pradīpādinivartyam avidyātmakaṃ tu jñānajyotiṣā ityuktau yogamokṣau ||
children.translated_text: External darkness is removed by a lamp and the like, but that which has ignorance as its nature is removed by the lamp of knowledge; with this statement, yoga and liberation have been explained.
Space, time, and direction are formless; because they differ, by formlessness, from earth and the rest, which possess action, they are inactive.
From the word 'and,' the self too is inactive.

children.text: etenāmūrtatvena guṇāḥ karmāṇi ca niṣkriyāṇi draṣṭavyāni caśabdāt sāmānyādayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: By this formlessness, qualities and actions too are to be understood as inactive; and, from the word 'and,' universals and the rest as well.

children.text: niṣkriyāṇām abhighātādīnāṃ karma samavetaṃ na bhavati svāśraye karmajananāt ||
children.translated_text: Action does not inhere in inactive things such as impact, because action produces action in its own substratum.
For that whose qualities have been stated as causes, they are causes only as non-inherent causes.

children.text: pūrveṇa niṣkramaṇam ityādeḥ pratyayabhedasya diṅ nimittakāraṇaṃ vyākhyātā kāraṇatvenātideśo nāsamavāyitvena ||
children.translated_text: By the preceding statement, direction has been explained as the instrumental cause of differences in cognition such as 'going out' and so on; the extension is with respect to causality, not with respect to being a non-inherent cause.

children.text: yenaiva kāraṇena pratyayabhedahetutvena dig vyākhyātā tenaiva yugapat kṛtam ityādi pratyayabhedasya kālo nimittakāraṇaṃ vyākhyātaḥ ||
children.translated_text: By the very same reason by which direction was explained as the cause of differences in cognition, time is explained as the instrumental cause of differences in cognition such as 'done simultaneously' and so on.

children.text: agnihotraṃ juhuyāt svargakāmaḥ ityevaṃbhūtā racanā bhagavato maheśvarasya buddhipūrvā sā tataḥ pramāṇam āptapraṇītatvasya satyatāvyāpteḥ ||
children.translated_text: A construction such as 'One who desires heaven should perform the <s>agnihotra</s>' is intentional, belonging to the blessed <s>Maheśvara</s>; therefore it is a means of valid knowledge, since being composed by a trustworthy person is pervaded by truth.
If it is objected that what is beyond the senses cannot be known:
A mark is cognition, because by it an object is indicated.

children.text: na hi yādṛśamasmadvijñānaṃ vartamānāvyavahitasambaddhārthaviṣayaṃ tādṛśameva bhagavato vijñānam ||
children.translated_text: For the cognition of the blessed one is not exactly like our cognition, whose object is something presently and immediately connected.
Therefore it is possible that the blessed one has cognition whose object is beyond the senses.

children.text: vinopadeśena brāhmaṇādikam artham asmākam ālocayatāṃ pratyakṣeṇa na brāhmaṇo'yam iti jñānamutpadyate ||
children.translated_text: When we consider, without instruction, the meaning of 'Brahmin' and the like, no knowledge arises through perception that 'this is a Brahmin.'
And, after an object has been considered by perception, the establishment of a name is seen in cases such as sons and the like.
