children.text: santi caitā brāhmaṇādisaṃjñās tā yena pratyakṣamarthamālocya praṇītā iti sūtrārthaṃ varṇayanti ||
children.translated_text: And these names such as 'Brahmin' do exist; commentators explain the meaning of the sūtra as that they were established by the one who considered the perceptible object by direct perception.

children.text: yata eva parameśvarasya kṛtirvedādau vākyapadaracanāto 'yaṃ smārto 'pi dānādividhis tadīyam āmnāyam anantaśākhābhinnam ālocya saṃkṣepamanumanyamānānāṃ bhṛguprabhṛtīnāṃ buddhipūrvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Precisely because the arrangement of sentences and words in the Veda and so on is the work of <s>Parameśvara</s>, this remembered injunction concerning gifts and the like is also intentional on the part of <s>Bhṛgu</s> and others, who, having examined his tradition divided into endless branches, approved an abridgement.
Thus injunctions concerning gifts and the like are causes of <s>dharma</s>.

children.text: tathaiva pratigraho'pi prakṣīṇavṛtteravadātajanmanaḥ pratigrahānurūpaguṇayuktasya dharmāyaiva bhavati ||
children.translated_text: In the same way, accepting a gift too becomes only for <s>dharma</s> when it is done by one whose livelihood has failed, whose birth is pure, and who possesses qualities appropriate for receiving.

children.text: yathā bhūtāni anitaretarāṅgaṃ na paraspareṇa kāryakāraṇabhūtāni na hyaraṇī agneḥ kāraṇam api tu svāvayavā eva atha cāraṇyoragneśca kramaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Just as the elements are not mutually ancillary to one another and are not causes and effects of one another, for the fire-sticks are not the cause of fire, but rather its own parts are; and yet there is a sequence between the fire-sticks and fire.

children.text: evametayoḥ pūrvaṃ dānadharmaḥ paścāt pratigrahadharmaḥ na tu kāryakāraṇabhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: So too, between these two, the <s>dharma</s> of giving comes first and the <s>dharma</s> of receiving afterward; but there is no relation of cause and effect.
Why?

children.text: na hyanyadīyā ātmaguṇā anyadīyātmaguṇānāṃ kāraṇaṃ bhavanti ||
children.translated_text: For qualities of one self do not become the causes of qualities of another self.

children.text: aduṣṭaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ bhojayitvā tadīyād āśīrvādādisamabhivyāhārāt puruṣābhyudayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: After feeding an uncorrupt Brahmin, a person's prosperity arises from the utterance of his blessing and the like.
The meaning is that <s>dharma</s> becomes the cause of that.

children.text: satyapyāśīrvādādivacane duṣṭaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ bhojayitvābhyudayo na prāpyate ||
children.translated_text: Even when words of blessing and the like are present, after feeding a corrupt Brahmin, prosperity is not obtained.

children.text: parasya hiṃsāyāṃ śarīramānasaduḥkharūpāyāṃ pravṛttaṃ duṣṭaṃ jānīṣva ||
children.translated_text: Know as corrupt one who is engaged in harming another, harm being bodily and mental pain.
The word 'harm' is indicative, since:

children.text: kṛtamahāpātakasya saṃbhāṣaṇamātrādeva doṣeṇa yujyate kimuta bhojanādinā iha samabhivyāhāraḥ sambhāṣaṇam pūrvatrāśīrvādaḥ ||
children.translated_text: One who has committed a great sin is joined with fault merely from conversation; how much more from feeding and the like. Here 'associated utterance' means conversation, while earlier it meant blessing.

children.text: tat samabhivyāhāradūṣaṇaṃ hiṃsādirahite brāhmaṇe na vidyate ||
children.translated_text: That defilement through associated utterance is not present in a Brahmin free from harm and the like.

children.text: na hiṃsādimātrarahite api tu deśakālavijñānācārair viśiṣṭe brāhmaṇe 'bhyudayārthinaḥ pravṛttiḥ ||
children.translated_text: The activity of one seeking prosperity is not toward a Brahmin merely free from harm and the like, but toward one distinguished by knowledge of place and time and by conduct.
Therefore:
An uncorrupt Brahmin, endowed with place and the rest, is called distinguished.
One endowed with one of these qualities is equal.
One endowed with all of them is distinguished.

children.text: tau tyaktvānyo duṣṭo vā kṣatriyādir vā prāṇimātraṃ vā hīna ucyate ||
children.translated_text: Apart from those two, another, whether corrupt, a Kṣatriya and so on, or merely any living being, is called inferior.

children.text: tatrābhyudayepsor mantrapūrvake suvarṇādidāne vaiśākhyādinimitte samahīnayorapravṛttiḥ api tu viśiṣṭe ||
children.translated_text: In that case, for one seeking prosperity, when giving gold and the like preceded by mantras on an occasion such as the month of <s>Vaiśākha</s>, there is no activity toward an equal or inferior recipient, but rather toward a distinguished one.
By this, taking another's property in distress is explained in the reverse order.
And it has been said:

children.text: hīnād ādeyam ādau tu tadabhāve samādapi
children.translated_text: First one should take from an inferior person; in his absence, even from an equal.
But if that is impossible, one may take even from a righteous distinguished person.

children.text: anenaiva viparītakrameṇa brāhmaṇa ātmano hīnai ripubhirmāraṇāyākṣiptastāneva śatrūnabhihanyāt ||
children.translated_text: By this same reverse order, when a Brahmin is attacked by enemies inferior to himself for the purpose of being killed, he should strike down those very enemies.

children.text: ātmanastulyaguṇena śatruṇā prāptasya brāhmaṇasya vikalpaḥ ātmano vadha ātatāyino vā ||
children.translated_text: For a Brahmin who is attacked by an enemy equal in qualities to himself, there is an option: his own killing, or that of the aggressor.

children.text: ātmano'dhikaguṇena śatruṇā prāptasyātmana eva ripuprayukto vadho'ṅgīkāryaḥ ||
children.translated_text: When a person has been attacked by an enemy whose qualities exceed his own, the killing of that person, brought about by the enemy, must be admitted.
Here, in the case of receiving gifts, the usage of being inferior and so on, with reference to the self, is relative among the recipients of gifts themselves.

children.text: śrutismṛtiparidṛṣṭānāṃ snānādīnāṃ dṛṣṭasya malāpakarṣāder anabhisaṃdhāne prayogo'bhyudayāya bhavati ||
children.translated_text: The performance of bathing and the like, which are seen in scripture and tradition, conduces to prosperity when there is no intention toward a visible purpose such as removing dirt.
Bathing is the conjunction of the body with water, depending on a specific place and time; that is ablution.
Fasting is the observance, preceded by a rule, in the form of not eating, whether by night or by day.

children.text: brahmaśabdena ātmā brahmaṇi caraṇamātmamanasor yaḥ saṃyogaḥ stryādiparihārarūpo brahmacaryam ||
children.translated_text: By the word <s>brahman</s> the self is meant; conduct in <s>brahman</s>, the conjunction of self and mind, in the form of avoiding women and the like, is <s>brahmacarya</s>.
Residence in the teacher's household by one who seeks knowledge and the like and is devoted to service of the teacher is residence in the <s>gurukula</s>.

children.text: śāstravidhinā gehānniḥsṛtyāraṇyaṃ prasthito vānaprasthaḥ tasya karma vānaprasthyam ||
children.translated_text: One who, according to scriptural rule, has gone forth from the house and set out for the forest is a <s>vānaprastha</s>; his action is the forest-dweller's practice.
Sacrifices are the cooked-offering sacrifices and the like.
Giving is the giving of gold and the like, and also the giving of safety.
Sprinkling is twilight worship and the like.
Other specifications are rules concerning direction and so on.
A rule concerning direction is: one should eat food facing east.
A rule concerning a lunar mansion is: one should place the fire when the <s>Kṛttikās</s> are present.
A rule concerning a mantra is: he offers with the words, 'of the god, you...'.
A rule concerning time is: a Brahmin should establish the fires in spring.

children.text: evametat sarvaṃ dṛṣṭaprayojanatiraskāreṇa prayujyamānaṃ dharmāya sampadyata iti ||
children.translated_text: Thus all this, when performed with disregard for a visible purpose, comes to be for the sake of <s>dharma</s>.

children.text: yadidaṃ caturṇāmāśramiṇāṃ karma tadupadhayā prayujyamānam adharmāyānupadhayā tu dharmāya bhavati
children.translated_text: Whatever action belongs to the four orders of life, when performed with an ulterior condition, is for <s>adharma</s>; but without such a condition it is for <s>dharma</s>.
What is an ulterior condition?
The meaning is that a fault such as hypocrisy in the disposition, that is, in the intention, is an ulterior condition.
What is absence of an ulterior condition?
The meaning is that absence of hypocrisy and the like in the intention is absence of an ulterior condition.

children.text: smṛtau yasya rūpādayo na niṣiddhāstacchuci mantrapūrvakaṃ prokṣitaṃ kevalābhir adbhir abhyukṣitaṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: That whose color and the like are not prohibited in tradition, and which is pure, sprinkled with mantra beforehand, and also sprinkled with plain water, is pure.
What is opposite to this is impure.
Moreover:
And that for which there is an absolute prohibition on purity is also impure, such as what is polluted by speech and the like.
And liquor and the like, whatever is directly prohibited, is also impure.
Therefore what is pure should be eaten.
Objection:

children.text: ayatasya viśiṣṭaprayatnarahitasya śucim āhāraṃ yadṛcchayopayuñjānasya abhyudayo nāsti viśiṣṭasyābhisaṃdher abhāvāt ||
children.translated_text: For one who is not disciplined, lacking a special effort, and who happens to consume pure food, there is no prosperity, because a specific intention is absent.
This is not so.

children.text: na prayatnavyatirekī yamaḥ prayatnābhāve sarvasyāḥ kriyāyā abhāvād vidyate śucim āhāram upayuñjānasya prayatnaḥ ||
children.translated_text: There is no restraint apart from effort; since, in the absence of effort, every action is absent, effort exists in one who consumes pure food.

children.text: yadi prayatnaḥ pradhānam vināpi yogādinābhyudayaḥ syāt ||
children.translated_text: If effort were principal, prosperity would occur even without yoga and the like.
This is not so.

children.text: asati yogādyanuṣṭhāne na prayatnamātrasya bhāvādabhyudayaḥ kriyopadeśavaiyarthyāt ||
children.translated_text: When the practice of yoga and the like is absent, prosperity does not arise merely from the existence of effort, because then the injunction of action would be pointless.
Now he states <s>dharma</s> as the cause of the highest good.
Attachment increases precisely from pleasure produced by women and other sense-objects.

children.text: yair yair asya sukhahetubhiḥ śarīraṃ bhāvitaṃ tanmaya ivāste ||
children.translated_text: By whichever causes of pleasure this body of his is conditioned, he remains as though made of them.
From that, because of being made of them, there is attachment.
Moreover:

children.text: yadā tṛpto bhavati tadāsya tṛptinimitto rāgo bhavati śarīrapuṣṭeḥ ||
children.translated_text: When he is satisfied, then he has attachment caused by that satisfaction, because of the nourishment of the body.
Moreover:

children.text: apūrvadṛṣṭeṣvanupakārakeṣu ca kasyacid rāgo jāyate'trādṛṣṭa eva kāraṇam ||
children.translated_text: In regard to things never seen before and things that are of no benefit, attachment arises in someone; here the unseen potency alone is the cause.
Moreover:

children.text: yathā tiraścāṃ tṛṇādibhojane evaṃ jātiviśeṣādapi rāgaḥ ||
children.translated_text: As among animals there is attachment to eating grass and the like, so attachment also arises from a particular birth-species.
From pleasure and the like comes attachment; from pain and the like comes aversion.
Therefore:

children.text: icchāpūrvikā dharme pravṛttiḥ anyena dhanamadādabhibhūtasya vā dveṣapūrvikāpi grāmakāmeṣṭyādau ||
children.translated_text: Activity toward <s>dharma</s> is preceded by desire; or, for one overpowered by the intoxication of wealth because of another, it may also be preceded by aversion, as in an offering made by one who desires a village.
In <s>adharma</s> too, activity is preceded by desire in regard to others' wives and the like, and preceded by aversion.
In this way there is accumulation of <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>.
Since this is so:

children.text: saṃcitau yadā dharmādharmau bhavataḥ tadā śarīrendriyaiḥ saṃyogo janmākhyo bhavati kṣīṇayośca tayormaraṇakāle viyogaḥ ||
children.translated_text: When <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> have been accumulated, then a conjunction with body and senses called birth occurs; and when those two are exhausted, at the time of death there is separation.

children.text: punarapyābhyāṃ dharmādharmābhyāṃ śarīrādisaṃyogo vibhāgaścetyevam anādir ayaṃ ghaṭīyantravadāvartate jantuḥ ||
children.translated_text: Again, through these two, <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>, there is conjunction with body and so on, and separation; thus this living being revolves beginninglessly like a water-wheel.
The opposite sequence is now stated; thus:

children.text: ātmeti manaḥ manaḥkarmasu tadabhāve saṃyogābhāvo'prādurbhāvaśca sa mokṣa iti mokṣo vyākhyātaḥ ||
children.translated_text: In the statement beginning 'self, mind,' when there is absence of that in the actions of the mind, there is absence of conjunction and non-manifestation; that is liberation. Thus liberation has been explained.
The meaning is that they were indicated by the sūtra on color and the rest.

children.text: dravyāśrayī ityādinā dravyakarmabhyāṃ vaidharmyaṃ kathitam ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The meaning is that by the statement beginning 'having substance as its substratum,' dissimilarity from substance and action has been stated.
For so it has been said: 'Earth possesses color, taste, smell, and touch,' and so on.
On this point:

children.text: ghaṭādeḥ pārthivasya dravyasya vināśāt tadgatānāmapi rūpādīnāṃ vināśa āśrayavināśāt ||
children.translated_text: Because an earthy substance such as a pot is destroyed, the color and other qualities present in it are also destroyed, since their substratum is destroyed.

children.text: agnisaṃyogācca pārthiveṣu paramāṇuṣu rūpādīnāṃ vināśaḥ kārye samavetānāṃ tvāśrayaparamāṇuṣvagnisaṃyogād eva kutaḥ ||
children.translated_text: And because of conjunction with fire, color and the other qualities are destroyed in earthy atoms; but how could the destruction of those inhering in the effect arise merely from the conjunction of fire with the atoms that are their substrata?

children.text: yasmācchyāmādiguṇebhyo vyatiriktaṃ guṇāntaramutpadyate tataḥ pūrve paramāṇuguṇā vinaṣṭāḥ guṇavati guṇānārambhāt ||
children.translated_text: Since another quality, distinct from dark color and the like, is produced, therefore the previous atomic qualities have been destroyed, because qualities do not initiate qualities in something already possessing qualities.

children.text: etena guṇāntaraprādurbhāvena nityeṣu paramāṇuṣu rūpādīnāmanityatvamuktaṃ pārthiveṣveva ||
children.translated_text: By this manifestation of another quality, the impermanence of color and the like in eternal atoms has been stated, and only in earthy atoms.
Because:

children.text: salilānalānilaparamāṇurūpādayo nityā āśrayanityatvād virodhiguṇāntarāprādurbhāvācca nāgnisaṃyogād vināśaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Color and the other qualities in atoms of water, fire, and air are eternal, because their substrata are eternal and because no other contrary quality comes into manifestation; therefore they are not destroyed by conjunction with fire.

children.text: anityeṣu salilādiṣu anityā rūpādaya āśrayavināśe teṣāmapi vināśāt ||
children.translated_text: In non-eternal things such as water, color and the other qualities are non-eternal, since when their substratum is destroyed they too are destroyed.

children.text: anityāyāṃ kāryarūpāyāṃ pṛthivyāṃ kāraṇaguṇapūrvā rūpādayo jāyante nityāyāṃ tu paramāṇusvabhāvāyāṃ pākajāḥ pākād agnisaṃyogājjātāḥ ||
children.translated_text: In an impermanent earth that is an effect, color and the like arise preceded by the qualities of the cause; but in the eternal earth, whose nature is atomic, they are produced by cooking, born from cooking, that is, from conjunction with fire.

children.text: kārye udakādyavayavini samavāyikāraṇarūpe rūpādaya ārabhyante pākajāstu jalādyaṇuṣu naiva santi virodhiguṇāntarābhāvāt ||
children.translated_text: In an effect, a composite whole such as water, color and the like are initiated in the form of the inhering cause; but qualities produced by cooking do not exist at all in water-atoms and the like, because there is no other contrary quality.

children.text: aguṇasya dravyasyaivotpannasya kāraṇaguṇairguṇā janyante na guṇakarmaṇām aśeṣāvayavaguṇaikārthasamavāyābhāvāt karmatvavat ||
children.translated_text: Only in a substance that has arisen without qualities are qualities produced by the qualities of the causes; they are not produced in qualities and actions, because there is no inherence in one and the same object with all the qualities of the parts, just as in the case of actionhood.

children.text: agnisaṃyogānnivṛtteṣu śyāmādiṣu pākajā jāyante iti te'pi guṇarahite siddhāḥ ||
children.translated_text: When dark color and the like have ceased because of conjunction with fire, cooked qualities arise; therefore they too are established in something devoid of qualities.

children.text: saṃyogavati saṃyogārambhavad guṇavati pākajā iti cenna ||
children.translated_text: If it is said that cooked qualities arise in something already possessing qualities, just as conjunction begins in something already possessing conjunction, no.

children.text: ekadravyavantaḥ pākajāste kathaṃ tatraivārabhyeran viruddhatvāt saṃyogasya tu saṃyogavatyārambho na duṣyati anekadravyatvāt ||
children.translated_text: Those cooked qualities have a single substance as their substratum; how could they be initiated in that very same place, since they would be opposed? But the initiation of conjunction in what already has conjunction is not faulty, because conjunction has many substances as its substratum.
Now we shall speak of measure.

children.text: nitye ityadhyāyanāma yadupalabhyate tatrāvaśyaṃ mahattvam aṇutve tu paramāṇudvyaṇukamanasāmanupalabdhiḥ evaṃ nityākhye'dhyāye upalabdhyanupalabdhyoḥ kāraṇe mahattvāṇutve kathite bhavataḥ upalabdhau mahattvasya niyamāt ||
children.translated_text: In the chapter named 'In the eternal,' whatever is perceived must have largeness; but with smallness there is non-perception of atoms, dyads, and mind. Thus in the chapter called 'eternal,' largeness and smallness have been stated as causes of perception and non-perception, because largeness is invariably present in perception.
Even when a triad has largeness, there is non-perception.

children.text: tryaṇuke tatkāraṇadvyaṇukagatā bahutvasaṃkhyā mahattvaṃ janayati kāraṇānāmamahattvāt ||
children.translated_text: In a triad, the number plurality belonging to its causal dyads produces largeness, because the causes are not large.
In something two fingers long, the largeness of the causal finger-measures produces largeness.
A loose conjunction is accumulation.
In two cotton masses, the accumulation present in the lumps of cotton, depending on the loose conjunction of the parts that are its substrata, initiates largeness.

children.text: etasmāt trikāraṇānmahato yad viparītaṃ dvyaṇukaparimāṇaṃ tadaṇu pratyetavyam ||
children.translated_text: From this threefold cause of largeness, whatever is opposite, namely the measure of a dyad, should be understood as small.

children.text: tasmin mahati vastuni kuvalādāv āmalakāpekṣayā aṇuvyavahāraḥ āmalake tu bilvāpekṣayā ||
children.translated_text: In that large object, such as a jujube, usage as 'small' occurs in comparison with an āmalaka; and in the case of an āmalaka, in comparison with a bilva.
Thus, through the presence or absence of greater degree, the usage 'small' and 'large' with regard to one and the same thing is figurative.
Why?

children.text: yata ekasminneva kāle tasminneva vastuni anyāpekṣayā dvau puruṣāvaṇumahadvyavahāraṃ viruddhaṃ kurvāte'to jānīmahe bhākto'yam iti ||
children.translated_text: Because at one and the same time, with regard to that very same object, two men make the opposed usages 'small' and 'large' in comparison with different things; therefore we know that this usage is figurative.
There, in the relatively small thing:

children.text: yathā śuklatantujanite kārye śuklimaiva na kṛṣṇatā evamato dṛṣṭāntānmahadbhir ārabdhe mahattvameva nāṇutvam ||
children.translated_text: Just as in an effect produced from white threads there is only whiteness and not blackness, so from this example, in what is begun by large causes, there is only largeness, not smallness.

children.text: yathā guṇakarmāṇi nirguṇāni kāryasya rūpāder avayavaguṇair ekārthasamavāyābhāvād evaṃ kāraṇabahutvādibhir ekārthasamavāyābhāvād aṇutvamahattvayos tadabhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Just as qualities and actions are without qualities, because there is no inherence in one and the same object with the qualities of the parts of an effect such as color, so because there is no inherence in one and the same object with causal plurality and the like, smallness and largeness are absent in them.

children.text: kāraṇabahutvādibhir ekārthasamavāyābhāvād aṇutvamahattve yathā aṇutvamahattvaśūnye evaṃ karmaguṇā aṇutvamahattvaśūnyāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Because there is no inherence in one and the same object with causal plurality and the like, smallness and largeness are, as it were, devoid of smallness and largeness; in the same way, actions and qualities are devoid of smallness and largeness.
Perception and non-perception are like largeness and smallness.

children.text: kāraṇamahattvādibhyaśca jāyate dīrghatvam viparītaṃ hrasvatvam tasmin viśeṣabhāvādityaupacārikatvaṃ tathaiva ||
children.translated_text: Length too arises from causal largeness and the like; the opposite is shortness. Since there is a special distinction in that case, the figurative character is just the same.
The extension is that length and shortness are absent in those two.

children.text: yathā kāraṇabahutvādyekārthasamavāyābhāvād aṇutvamahattvaśūnyā evaṃ dīrghatvahrasvatvaśūnyā ete karmaguṇāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Just as they are devoid of smallness and largeness because there is no inherence in one and the same object with causal plurality and the like, so these actions and qualities are devoid of length and shortness.
This fourfold measure, because it exists in the non-eternal, is non-eternal.
But:
The measure of an atom is spherical; that is eternal.
Of that:

children.text: parimāṇarahitasya dravyasyāsambhavaḥ paramāṇūnāṃ paramāṇuparimāṇasya sambhave liṅgam ||
children.translated_text: The impossibility of a substance without measure is the sign for the existence of atomic measure in atoms.
Non-existence is ignorance; existence is knowledge.

children.text: vibhavānmūrtadravyaiḥ samāgatairagacchataḥ saṃyogāt paramamahattvam ākāśasyāstīti gamyate ||
children.translated_text: Because space is all-pervading, from its conjunction with corporeal substances that come together while it does not move, it is understood that space has supreme largeness.
Like space, the self too should be regarded as supremely large.
Since direction and time are not composite, they too are large.
Because it is not all-pervading, and because cognitions are not simultaneous, mind is atomic.

children.text: yatra yatrāvadhiṃ karoti tatra tatra idamasmāt pūrveṇa ityādivyavahāro mūrteṣu pravartate ato mūrtasaṃyogākhyair guṇair dig vyākhyātā mahattvavatī ||
children.translated_text: Wherever it sets a limit, there the usage among corporeal things, such as 'this is east of that,' occurs; therefore direction, explained by the qualities called conjunction with corporeal things, possesses largeness.
Likewise:

children.text: yena kāraṇena parāparavyatikarādinā kālo'numīyate tasya sarvatra bhāvāt tenaiva kāraṇena kālo vibhurvyākhyātaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The cause by which time is inferred, such as the intermixture of prior and posterior, exists everywhere; therefore by that same cause time is explained as all-pervading.
The cognition 'this is one' and the like is not caused by color and the like, because it is distinct from cognitions of those.
For a cognition caused by color and the like would be a cognition such as 'it has color.'
Therefore it is caused by another object.
Unity and single separateness in effects are preceded by the qualities of their causes.
Duality and the rest arise from unities accompanied by a cognition whose object is more than one.
The same applies to separateness beginning with dual separateness, in relation to the separatenesses; but there is absence of any further universal such as single-separateness and so on.

children.text: yathā dravyanityatvāt tejaḥparamāṇurūpasparśau nityau evam ekatvaikapṛthaktve nityadravyavartinī nitye yathā cānitye tejasi dravyānityatvād anityau rūpasparśau tathaiva kāryavartinī anitye ekatvaikapṛthaktve ||
children.translated_text: Just as, because substance is eternal, the color and touch of a fire-atom are eternal, so unity and single-separateness, when they occur in eternal substances, are eternal; and just as in non-eternal fire, because the substance is non-eternal, color and touch are non-eternal, so unity and single-separateness, when they occur in effects, are non-eternal.

children.text: yathā ca tejasi kārye kāraṇaguṇapūrvā rūpasparśayorutpattir evam ekatvapṛthaktvayoḥ ||
children.translated_text: And just as, in fire as an effect, the arising of color and touch is preceded by the qualities of the cause, so it is with unity and separateness.
So too with heaviness, fluidity, and viscidity.
Because there is no inherence in one and the same object along with the qualities of the parts in the case of unity and separateness, there are not unity and separateness there; this is the meaning.
In the same way, because there is no inherence in one and the same object along with the qualities of the parts, actions and qualities do not possess unity and separateness.
Objection: all categories have unity, because there is no difference with respect to being existent.

children.text: karmaṇāṃ guṇānāṃ ca saṃkhyārahitatvāt sarvaikatvaṃ naivāsti ||
children.translated_text: Since actions and qualities are devoid of number, there is certainly no unity of everything.
If one says that there is a figurative unity in qualities and the like,

children.text: mukhyasyaikatvasyābhāvād guṇādiṣu bhāktaṃ yadekatvaṃ kalpyate tad bhavata ekatvasiddhau na paryāpnoti dravyeṣu mukhyam guṇeṣu bhāktam ityata eva bhedaprasaṅgāt ||
children.translated_text: then, since principal unity is absent, the figurative unity imagined in qualities and the like is not sufficient for establishing unity for you; for precisely because one would say, 'principal in substances, figurative in qualities,' a difference would follow.

children.text: nanu kāryakāraṇayor ekatvaṃ prāptaṃ dravye saṃkhyānirviśeṣāt ekatvābhāvādeva pṛthaktvabhāvaḥ syāt ||
children.translated_text: Objection: unity between effect and cause would follow, since in substance there is no distinction of number; and because unity is absent, separateness itself would exist.
This is not so.

children.text: dvitvāt kāryakāraṇayor naikatvaṃ kāryasya kāraṇavyatiriktāśrayābhāvān nāpi pṛthaktvam ||
children.translated_text: Because effect and cause are two, there is no unity between them; and since the effect has no substratum apart from the cause, there is also no separateness.
This preceding sūtra, though concerned with non-eternal things, should also be understood as explained, as far as possible, in eternal things such as ether.

children.text: tathāhi śabdākāśayoḥ kāryakāraṇayor naikatvaṃ nāpi pṛthaktvam ||
children.translated_text: Thus, between sound and ether, as effect and cause, there is neither unity nor separateness.
Conjunction produced by the action of one of the two occurs between a <s>śyena</s> and a post, through the approaching action of the <s>śyena</s>.
Conjunction produced by both occurs through the approaching of two wrestlers.

children.text: saṃyogajaḥ kāraṇākāraṇayoḥ saṃyogāt kāryākāryagataḥ yathāṅgulyākāśasaṃyogābhyāṃ dvyaṅgulākāśasaṃyogaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Conjunction produced by conjunction, belonging to an effect and a non-effect, arises from the conjunction of a cause and a non-cause, as the conjunction of two fingers with ether arises from the conjunctions of each finger with ether.
Disjunction produced by the action of one of the two occurs from the moving away of a <s>śyena</s>.
Disjunction produced by the action of both occurs from the moving away of two rams.

children.text: vibhāgajastu aṅgulyoranyonyavibhāgād vinaṣṭamātre dvyaṅgule'ṅgulyākāśavibhāgaḥ kāraṇākāraṇayorvā hastākāśayor vibhāgāccharīrākāśavibhāgaḥ ||
children.translated_text: But disjunction produced by disjunction occurs, when the two-finger measure has just been destroyed, as the disjunction of the fingers from ether from the mutual disjunction of the fingers; or, between a cause and a non-cause, as the disjunction of the body from ether from the disjunction of the hand from ether.
Because there is no independent establishment in separation, those two do not exist; this is the meaning.
Because there is no independent establishment in separation, they do not possess conjunction and disjunction; this is the meaning.

children.text: kāryakāraṇayoḥ paraspareṇa saṃyogavibhāgau na vidyete yathā ghaṭakapālayoḥ yutasiddhyabhāvāt ||
children.translated_text: There is no conjunction or disjunction of effect and cause with each other, as in the case of a pot and its potsherds, because there is no independent establishment in separation.

children.text: yutasiddhir dvayor anyatarasya vā pṛthaggatimattvam sā ca nityayoḥ yutāśrayasamavetatvaṃ cānityayoḥ yathā ghaṭapaṭayoḥ tvagindriyapārthivaśarīrayośca ||
children.translated_text: Independent establishment in separation is the possession of separate motion by two things, or by one of them; and it is, in the case of eternal things, inherence in conjoined substrata, and, in the case of non-eternal things, inherence in substrata that are conjoined, as with a pot and a cloth, and with the skin-sense and an earthy body.

children.text: na ca ghaṭakapālayoḥ yutāśrayasamavāyaḥ ghaṭasya teṣveva samavetatvāt ||
children.translated_text: And there is no inherence in conjoined substrata for the pot and its potsherds, because the pot inheres in those very potsherds.
If it is said that sound has a relation with its meaning, no.
Because sound is a quality of ether, it is not related to the meaning.

children.text: guṇe ca rūpaṃ rasa ityādiṣu prayujyate kriyāyāṃ ca na ca guṇakarmaṇāṃ guṇaiḥ sambandhaḥ ||
children.translated_text: And a word is used with reference to a quality, as in 'color' and 'taste,' and also with reference to an action; but qualities and actions have no relation with qualities.

children.text: arthasaṃyoge sati śabdo'rthaṃ prāpnuyāt niṣkriyatvācca guṇasya gamanābhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: If sound were in conjunction with the meaning, sound would reach the meaning; and because a quality is inactive, there is no motion.

children.text: arthasaṃyoge sati śabdaḥ asati abhāve nāsti iti na prayujyeta ||
children.translated_text: If sound were in conjunction with the meaning, then in the absence of the meaning it would not be used in expressions such as 'it is not' or 'there is no existent thing.'
For there is no conjunction with what is nonexistent.
Therefore, because conjunction is absent,
But one may object:
A cognition of a staff-bearer and of a horned animal is seen from the staff and horns, which are respectively conjoined and inherent.

children.text: asti ca śabdād arthapratyayaḥ tasmādasyāpi sambandho'stīti ||
children.translated_text: And there is cognition of a meaning from a word; therefore this too has a relation.
This is not so.

children.text: daṇḍiviṣāṇinor dṛṣṭatvād adoṣaḥ iha tu śabdārthayoḥ sambandhasyoktanyāyenādṛṣṭatvādahetur arthapratyayaḥ sambandhe ||
children.translated_text: Since staff-bearers and horned animals are observed, there is no fault there; but here, since a relation between word and meaning is not observed according to the reasoning already stated, cognition of the meaning is not a reason for a relation.

children.text: yadi śabdo'rthena sambaddhaḥ syād agṛhītasaṃketo 'pi tato'rthaṃ pratipadyeta ||
children.translated_text: If a word were related to its meaning, even one who had not learned the convention would understand the meaning from it.
Therefore word and meaning are unrelated.

children.text: nanu śabdenākāśaṃ sambaddham ākāśena cārthaḥ evaṃ sambandhasambandhād arthena sambandha iti ||
children.translated_text: Objection: a word is related to ether, and ether is related to the meaning; thus, through relation to what is related, it is related to the meaning.

children.text: naitat sarvārthānāmākāśena sambandhāt kasminnarthe śabdaḥ prayukta iti sandehādapratipattiḥ syāt ||
children.translated_text: This is not so; since all meanings are related to ether, there would be uncertainty as to which meaning the word was used for, and no understanding would arise.
Therefore there is no relation.

children.text: tasmāt saṅketanimittaḥ śabdādarthe pratyayo na sambandhāt ||
children.translated_text: Therefore cognition of a meaning from a word has convention as its cause, not relation.
Two masses in the same direction are the cause of priority and posteriority produced by direction.
Two things at the same time, connected with the present time, are the cause of priority and posteriority produced by time.
And those two masses are the cause, in dependence on cognitions of nearness and remoteness.
Conjunction with regions of nearer and farther direction is the non-inherent cause.
Likewise, conjunctions with regions of nearer and farther time are the non-inherent causes.

children.text: dikkālapradeśaiḥ saṃyogāt saṃnikṛṣṭaviprakṛṣṭayoḥ piṇḍayoḥ saṃnikṛṣṭaviprakṛṣṭabuddhyapekṣayā saṃnikṛṣṭe'paratvam viprakṛṣṭe ca paratvam ||
children.translated_text: Because of conjunction with regions of direction and time, and in dependence on cognitions of nearness and remoteness regarding two masses that are near and remote, posteriority belongs to the nearer one and priority to the remote one.
Conjunctions with regions of farther and nearer direction and time are the cause of farness and nearness.
And since, because these two are not separately established, there is no conjunction, there is no farness or nearness in them.

children.text: yathā karmaguṇā aṇutvamahattvaśūnyā evaṃ karmaguṇā yutasiddhyabhāvena dikkālapradeśasaṃyogābhāvāt paratvāparatvaśūnyāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Just as actions and qualities are devoid of minuteness and greatness, so actions and qualities, because there is no conjunction with regions of direction and time owing to the absence of separate establishment, are devoid of farness and nearness.
Qualities and the rest inhere in substance.

children.text: ataḥ samavāyaṃ kathayati iheti yataḥ kāryakāraṇayoḥ pratyaya utpadyate iha tantuṣu paṭaḥ iha ghaṭe rūpādayaḥ iha ghaṭe karma iti sa samavāyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Therefore he explains <s>samavāya</s> (inherence): that from which the cognition 'here' arises with regard to effect and cause, as 'the cloth is here in the threads,' 'color and the like are here in the pot,' and 'action is here in the pot,' is <s>samavāya</s>.
This is because the mention of effect and cause serves as an indication.

children.text: jātervyaktau viśeṣāṇāṃ ca nityadravyeṣu samavāyaḥ ityuktaṃ bhavati ||
children.translated_text: The meaning is that there is <s>samavāya</s> of the universal in the individual, and of particularities in eternal substances.

children.text: yathaikadravyavattvānna dravyaṃ bhāvo guṇakarmasu ca bhāvānna karma na guṇa evaṃ samavāyo'pi ||
children.translated_text: As, because it has one substance, an existent among qualities and actions is not a substance, and because it exists among qualities and actions it is not an action nor a quality, so too <s>samavāya</s> is distinct.

children.text: yathā salliṅgāviśeṣād eko bhāvas tathā ihaliṅgāviśeṣādekaḥ samavāyo vṛttirahito nityo niravayavaśca ||
children.translated_text: Just as, because there is no difference in the mark 'existent,' existence is one, so, because there is no difference in the mark 'here,' <s>samavāya</s> is one, without further subsistence, eternal, and without parts.

children.text: ṣaṇṇāṃ padārthānāṃ madhyād dravyeṣveva jñānaṃ vyākhyātaṃ yathotpadyate sannikarṣāt na tu guṇādiṣu ||
children.translated_text: Among the six categories, knowledge with respect to substances alone has been explained: how it arises from contact, but not with respect to qualities and the rest.
Of that:

children.text: mana ātmā ca jñānasya kāraṇaṃ vyākhyātam ||
children.translated_text: Mind and self have been explained as causes of knowledge.
Now he states knowledge with respect to qualities and the rest.

children.text: yata indriyasannikarṣeṇa jñānaniṣpattiruktā guṇādīnāṃ cendriyeṇa sannikarṣo nāstītyatastvidānīṃ jñānamucyate teṣām asaṃnikarṣe vijñānaṃ yataḥ ||
children.translated_text: Since the production of knowledge has been stated as occurring through sense-contact, and qualities and the rest have no contact with a sense-organ, therefore knowledge of them is now stated: when they are not in contact, cognition arises because of that.

children.text: guṇakarmaṇāṃ yato dravyaṃ samavāyikāraṇaṃ tatasteṣu sākṣādindriyeṇāsaṃnikṛṣṭeṣu vijñānaniṣpatteḥ kāraṇasya sannikarṣasya tadeva dravyaṃ kāraṇaṃ na guṇakarmāṇi tasmād guṇakarmasu saṃyuktasamavāyājjñānam caśabdo hetau ||
children.translated_text: Since substance is the inherent cause of qualities and actions, that very substance, because of the production of cognition of them when they are not directly in contact with a sense-organ, is the cause of the contact that is the cause; qualities and actions are not. Therefore knowledge with respect to qualities and actions arises from inherence in what is conjoined. The word ca is causal.

children.text: sāmānye sattādau viśeṣeṣu cāntyeṣu taddarśināṃ dravyasannikarṣādeva jñānamutpadyate na sāmānyaviśeṣebhyaḥ teṣu tadabhāvāt
children.translated_text: With regard to universals such as existence, and to ultimate particulars, knowledge for those who perceive them arises only from contact with substance, not from universals and particulars, because that is absent in them.
But elsewhere:

children.text: dravyaguṇakarmasu dravyendriyasannikarṣāt sāmānyācca sādeḥ sāmānyaviśeṣācca dravyatvādeḥ sat iti dravyam ityādi ca jñānamutpadyata iti ||
children.translated_text: With respect to substances, qualities, and actions, from contact between a substance and a sense-organ, and from the universal such as existence and from the universal-particular such as substanceness, cognitions arise such as 'it is existent,' 'it is a substance,' and so on.

children.text: iha sūtre sāmānyaṃ sattā viśeṣā dravyatvādayaḥ pūrvasūtre'nyathā ||
children.translated_text: In this sūtra the universal is existence, and the particulars are substanceness and the like; in the previous sūtra it was otherwise.
There also:

children.text: cakṣuḥsannikarṣād yajjñānaṃ dravye sāmānyaviśeṣāpekṣaṃ viṣāṇī iti guṇāpekṣaṃ śuklaḥ iti karmāpekṣaṃ gacchati ityutpadyata iti ||
children.translated_text: From contact with the eye, knowledge arises in a substance as dependent on a universal-particular, as 'horned'; dependent on a quality, as 'white'; and dependent on an action, as 'it goes.'

children.text: dravyādīnāṃ ca viśeṣaṇatvāt pūrvamupalambhaḥ tena viśeṣaṇabuddheḥ kāraṇatvaṃ viśeṣyabuddheḥ kāryatvam ||
children.translated_text: And because substances and the rest function as qualifiers, they are apprehended first; therefore cognition of the qualifier is the cause, and cognition of the qualified is the effect.

children.text: guṇe guṇakarmaṇorabhāvāt karmaṇi ca guṇakarmanimittaṃ guṇakarmasu jñānaṃ na bhavatīti ||
children.translated_text: Since qualities and actions are absent in a quality, and since in an action knowledge of qualities and actions, having qualities and actions as its basis, does not occur with respect to qualities and actions.
There is no fixed rule about the prior arising of knowledge in regard to substance and the rest, as follows.

children.text: śvetaguṇasamavāyinaḥ śvaityasāmānyāt śvaityasāmānyajñānācca śvetaguṇajñānaṃ jāyate sāmānyaguṇasambandho'pi draṣṭavyaḥ ato viśeṣaṇabuddhiḥ kāraṇaṃ viśeṣyabuddhiḥ kāryam ||
children.translated_text: From the universal whiteness inhering in a white quality, and from knowledge of the universal whiteness, knowledge of the white quality arises; the relation between universal and quality too should be understood. Therefore cognition of the qualifier is the cause, and cognition of the qualified is the effect.
But in the relation of qualifier and qualified:

children.text: aṇutvān manaso yaugapadyābhāvāt satyapi krame ghaṭapaṭajñānayorna kāryakāraṇabhāvaḥ viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyatvāyogāt ||
children.translated_text: Because the mind is minute and simultaneity is impossible, even though there is sequence, there is no relation of effect and cause between the cognitions of pot and cloth, since they cannot stand as qualifier and qualified.

children.text: gauḥ śuklā gacchatīti ca dravyaguṇakarmasu jñānānāṃ krameṇāpi jāyamānānāṃ na ||
children.translated_text: And in the case 'the cow is white and goes,' the cognitions concerning substance, quality, and action, even though arising in sequence, are not
in a relation of effect and cause, because there is no relation of qualifier and qualified; this follows from the non-specificity of the reason stated before.

children.text: ato dravyajñānaṃ na guṇakarmabuddhyoḥ kāraṇam guṇakarmabuddhī api na parasya kāraṇam ||
children.translated_text: Therefore knowledge of substance is not the cause of cognitions of quality and action, nor are cognitions of quality and action causes of one another.
But where the rule of qualification is absent:

children.text: ayam iti saṃnikṛṣṭe eṣaḥ iti ca kiṃcid viprakṛṣṭe pratyayaḥ kṛtaṃ tvayā iti karmakartṛpratyayo bhojayainam iti kartṛkarmapratyayau ||
children.translated_text: There is the cognition 'this' with regard to what is in contact, and 'that' with regard to something somewhat remote; 'done by you' is a cognition of action and agent, and 'make him eat' contains cognitions of agent and object.

children.text: saṃnikṛṣṭāpekṣo viprakṛṣṭe pratyayaḥ kṛtam iti karmāpekṣaḥ kartari bhojaya iti kartrapekṣaḥ karmaṇi ||
children.translated_text: A cognition of what is remote depends on what is in contact; in 'done,' the agent depends on the action; in 'make eat,' the object depends on the agent.
If it is asked, 'Why are they dependent?'

children.text: dṛṣṭeṣu satsu yataḥ saṃnikṛṣṭādiṣu viprakṛṣṭādipratyayā bhavanti nādṛṣṭeṣu ataḥ sāpekṣā api santo na kāryakāraṇabhūtā viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyatvāyogāt ||
children.translated_text: Because cognitions of the remote and the like arise when things in contact and the like have been seen, not when they have not been seen. Thus, though they are dependent, they are not effects and causes, since they cannot stand as qualifier and qualified.
Although cognitions depend on objects and sense-organs, for the moment the object is stated.

children.text: vināpyarthatvena sāmānyena triṣveva dravyādiṣu tatra prasiddhyā arthaśabdaḥ paribhāṣyate ||
children.translated_text: Even without the general property of being an object, the word 'object' is conventionally defined in just the three, substance and the rest, because usage is established there.

children.text: kveva yathā sāmānyaviśeṣeṣu vinā sāmānyāntareṇa yathā sattādiṣu sāmānyeṣu sāmānyaṃ sāmānyam iti jñānaṃ tathā viśeṣeṣu viśeṣāntarābhāve'pi viśeṣo viśeṣaḥ iti taddarśināṃ vijñānamevaṃ dravyādiṣu vināpyarthatvena pāribhāṣiko 'rthaśabdaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Where exactly? Just as, with respect to universals and particulars, without another universal, there is for those who perceive them the cognition 'universal, universal' with respect to universals such as existence, and likewise the cognition 'particular, particular' with respect to particulars even without another particular; in the same way, with respect to substance and the rest, even without objecthood, the word 'object' is used conventionally.

children.text: indriyāṇyucyante tāni ca na pañcātmakāni yataḥ ||
children.translated_text: The sense-organs are now stated; and they are not composed of five elements, because:

children.text: yato dravyeṣvārabdhavyeṣu pañcabhūtānyārambhakāṇi na vidyante api tu yānyārabhante catvāri tāni svāṃ svāṃ jātimārabhante ||
children.translated_text: For, among the substances that are to be originated, the five elements are not the originating causes; rather, whichever four elements originate them, they originate each according to its own class.
In the same way, the senses too are effects of determinate elements. For so it is:

children.text: gandhajñānaṃ ghrāṇam tasminnārabdhavye pṛthivī kāraṇaṃ bhūyastvāt śarīrāpekṣayā tu bhūyastvam ||
children.translated_text: The organ of smell is the knowledge of smell. When it is to be originated, earth is the cause, because of predominance; but the predominance is in comparison with the body.

children.text: bhūyastvaṃ ca ghrāṇe pṛthivyāḥ pādādinā gandhopalabdhyabhāvāt ||
children.translated_text: And the predominance of earth in the organ of smell is established because smell is not apprehended by the foot and the like.

children.text: gandhavattvācca yataśca svasamavāyinā gandhena ghrāṇendriyaṃ gandhamabhivyanaktyatastasya gandhavatī pṛthivyeva kāraṇam bhūtāntarāṇi tu saṃyogīni svalpānyeva ||
children.translated_text: And because it possesses smell: since the organ of smell manifests smell by means of the smell inhering in itself, therefore fragrant earth alone is its cause. The other elements are merely conjoined with it, and are quite small in amount.

children.text: svasamavāyinā madhurāpākajena rasena rūpeṇa śuklabhāsvareṇa sparśena apākajānuṣṇā śītena yato rasanānayanasparśanāni rasarūpasparśānabhivyañjantyato rasavattvād rūpavattvāt sparśavattvācca bhūtāntarair nimittair anabhibhūtatvena bhūyastvācca triṣvindriyeṣu yathāsaṅkhyam āpas tejo vāyuśca samavāyikāraṇāni draṣṭavyāni ||
children.translated_text: Since the organs of taste, sight, and touch manifest taste, color, and touch respectively by means of the taste produced in cooking and sweet, the white and bright color, and the touch that is not produced in cooking and is neither hot nor cold, and since they possess taste, color, and touch, and because they are not overpowered by the other elements that serve as instrumental causes and because of predominance, water, fire, and air should be understood, in that order, as the inhering causes in the three senses.

children.text: ākāśaṃ tu svata eva śrotraṃ karṇaśaṣkulyavacchinnaṃ na prakṛtiranārambhakatvāt ||
children.translated_text: But ether, delimited by the cavity of the ear, is by itself the organ of hearing; it is not a material cause, because it does not originate anything.
Thus perception has been explained.

children.text: na tāvat kāryaṃ prāgutpatteḥ pratyakṣeṇa gṛhyate ||
children.translated_text: To begin with, an effect before its production is not grasped by perception.

children.text: nāpyanumānena sati liṅge tasya bhāvāt liṅgābhāvaśca tadīyayoḥ kriyāguṇayoranupalabdheḥ na cānyad vyapadeśaśabdasūcitaṃ liṅgamasti ||
children.translated_text: Nor is it grasped by inference, because, if there were an inferential mark, the thing would exist; and there is no inferential mark, since its actions and qualities are not apprehended. Nor is there any other inferential mark indicated by the word 'designation'.
Therefore, before production it is nonexistent.
Afterwards:

children.text: sadbhūtaṃ ca kāryaṃ pradhvastamuttarakālamasadeva na satastirodhānaṃ kriyāguṇavyapadeśābhāvād eva ||
children.translated_text: And an effect that has come into being, when it has been destroyed at a later time, is simply nonexistent; there is no concealment of what exists, precisely because action, quality, and designation are absent.
But in the middle:

children.text: pradhvaṃsāt pūrvam utpatter uttarakālam asato 'rthāntarabhūtaṃ vastu sat ityucyate kriyāguṇavyapadeśānāṃ bhāvāt ||
children.translated_text: Before destruction and after production, the thing, being distinct from what is nonexistent, is said to exist, because actions, qualities, and designations are present.

children.text: sadapi vastu bhāvāntaraniṣedhena gauraśvo na bhavatīti kāryākaraṇena nāyaṃ gauryo na vahati asat ityupacaryate ||
children.translated_text: Even an existent thing is figuratively called nonexistent through the denial of another state, as when one says, 'a cow is not a horse,' or through incapacity for an effect, as in, 'this cow does not carry' or 'it does not draw'.

children.text: sataśca vastuno yadanyadatyantābhāvarūpaṃ prāgupādhipradhvaṃsābhāvāviṣayaṃ śaśaviṣāṇādi tadapyasadeva ||
children.translated_text: And whatever is other than an existent thing, having the nature of absolute absence and not falling within prior absence, conditioned absence, or absence after destruction, such as a hare's horn and the like, that too is simply nonexistent.

children.text: asatāmaviśeṣāt prāgasati kathaṃ kārakapravṛttirnānyatreti cet na viśeṣagrahaṇāt ||
children.translated_text: If one objects, 'Since nonexistent things are without distinction, how is there activity of causal factors toward what is previously nonexistent, and not elsewhere?', the answer is: no, because a distinction is apprehended.

children.text: pradhvaṃsāsati asat iti jñānaṃ bhūtasya vastunaḥ pūrvavadidānīṃ darśanābhāvāt tasya ca bhūtasya vastunaḥ smaraṇād virodhinaśca kapālādergrahaṇād vināśaṃ parikalpyotpadyate anyathā tat kathamiva na dṛśyeta tathātvasyāviśeṣāt ||
children.translated_text: In the case of nonexistence after destruction, the cognition 'it is nonexistent' arises by recognizing the destruction of a thing that once existed: because it is now no longer seen as before, because that past thing is remembered, and because something opposed to it, such as potsherds, is apprehended. Otherwise, how would it not be seen, since its condition would be no different?
But in prior absence:

children.text: mṛtpiṇḍāvasthāyāṃ prāgabhāve ghaṭaviṣayaṃ pratyakṣajñānaṃ nābhūt idānīṃ tu ghaṭaviṣayaṃ viruddhaṃ vijñānamudabhūt smaryate cābhāvāvasthā tasmād idānīm ayaṃ bhāvaḥ samabhūt pūrvam asyābhāva eva cāsīditi prāgabhāve asat iti niścayajñānam ||
children.translated_text: In the state of a lump of clay, when there was prior absence, there was no perceptual cognition whose object was a pot; now, however, a contrary cognition whose object is a pot has arisen, and the state of absence is remembered. Therefore the determinate cognition arises, 'now this existent thing has come into being, and previously there was only its absence'; thus, in prior absence, it is known as nonexistent.

children.text: yadā hi sthālyāṃ ghaṭa ityutpannavijñānasya kāraṇāntarataḥ samyakpratyaya utpadyate nāyaṃ ghaṭaḥ sthālīyam iti tadapi ghaṭapratyayasyābhāvāt tasya ca smaraṇād viruddhasya ca sthālyāderdarśanād boddhavyam ||
children.translated_text: For when someone has the cognition 'there is a pot in the basin,' and from another cause a correct cognition arises, 'this is not a pot; it is this basin,' that too should be understood from the absence of the pot-cognition, from the memory of it, and from the sight of the opposed thing, namely the basin and so on.
Likewise, in the case of a horse, the cognition is 'not a cow'.

children.text: tathā sāmānyato darśanād rātrisnānāderdharmatve saṃbhāvite adharmaḥ ityutpadyata iti cetanācetanātīndriyabhedenodāharaṇatrayam ||
children.translated_text: Similarly, when from general observation bathing at night and the like has been considered possibly to be <s>dharma</s>, the cognition 'it is <s>adharma</s>' arises; thus there is a threefold set of examples, differentiated as conscious, unconscious, and supersensible.

children.text: prākpradhvaṃsopādhyabhāvebhyo yadatyantābhāvarūpaṃ śaśaviṣāṇādi tad abhūtam nāsti iti paryāyaśabdābhyāmavyatiriktamucyate nāsya paryāyaśabdair arthāntaratā kathyate ato 'sya paryāyaśabdairevopadarśanaṃ lakṣaṇam nāsya deśakālādiniṣedhaḥ ||
children.translated_text: That which has the nature of absolute absence, such as a hare's horn and the like, as distinct from prior absence, absence after destruction, and conditioned absence, is expressed without difference by the synonymous words 'not been' and 'does not exist'. No difference of meaning is stated for it by the synonymous words. Therefore its definition is indication simply by those synonymous words; it is not the negation of place, time, and so forth.
But elsewhere:

children.text: nāsti ghaṭo'smin deśe kāle veti deśādiniṣedho ghaṭādeḥ na svarūpato niṣedhaḥ kriyata iti ||
children.translated_text: When one says, 'there is no pot in this place or at this time,' this is a negation of place and the like for a pot and so forth; it is not a negation of its own nature.

children.text: nāsti dvitīyaś candramāḥ iti saṅkhyāpratiṣedhena sāmānyāccandratvākhyāccandramā nivartyate iti kṛtvā candratvaṃ sāmānyaṃ nāstītyuktaṃ bhavati ||
children.translated_text: In the statement, 'there is no second moon,' because the moon is excluded through the denial of number from the general property called moonhood, it amounts to saying that the universal moonhood does not exist.

children.text: deśakālabhāvasāmarthyopādhīnām abhāve tadatyantāsata eva prabhedaścandratvasāmānyaniṣedha iti varṇayanti ||
children.translated_text: They explain that, when the limiting conditions of place, time, existence, and capacity are absent, the negation of the universal moonhood is a subtype precisely of what is absolutely nonexistent.

children.text: sikatābhyo'nutpatterdadhnaḥ kṣīrāccotpatteḥ pratyakṣeṇa cāgrahaṇāt sadasat kāryaṃ kāraṇe ||
children.translated_text: Because curds do not arise from grains of sand, because they do arise from milk, and because they are not grasped by perception, the effect is both existent and nonexistent in the cause.
Since existence and nonexistence are mutually contradictory when simultaneous, the effect is not both existent and nonexistent in the cause.
Therefore it is nonexistent alone.
Because its objects are both perceptible and imperceptible, yogic perception is explained between perception and inference.

children.text: āhṛtya viṣayebhya indriyāṇi tebhyaśca mana ātmanyeva yadā samādhīyate tadā yogajadharmāpekṣād ātmāntaḥkaraṇasaṃyogād viśiṣṭāttatrabhavatāṃ svasminnātmani jñānaṃ pratyakṣam utpadyate ||
children.translated_text: When the senses have been withdrawn from their objects, and the mind from them, and it is concentrated only in the self, then, in dependence on dharma born of yoga and from a special conjunction of the self and the inner organ, direct cognition arises for those venerable persons in their own self.

children.text: pratiṣiddhātmasaṃyogeṣu vyāpakadravyeṣvātmanāsaṃyukteṣu apratiṣiddhātmasaṃyogeṣu ca paramāṇvādiṣūbhābhyāṃ saṃyukteṣu jñānamutpadyate ||
children.translated_text: In the case of pervasive substances, whose conjunction with the self is denied and which are not conjoined with the self, and also in the case of atoms and the like, whose conjunction with the self is not denied and which are conjoined with both, cognition arises.
Moreover:
With respect to subtle, hidden, and remote objects, direct perception arises for them even through the contact of the fourfold set.
Likewise in perceptions such as ours.

children.text: yathāntaḥkaraṇasaṃyogād dravyāntareṣu jñānamutpadyate tathaiva taddravyasamaveteṣu karmaguṇeṣu jñānamutpadyate ||
children.translated_text: Just as cognition arises, from conjunction with the inner organ, with respect to other substances, so too cognition arises with respect to actions and qualities inhering in those substances.

children.text: yathā ca catuṣṭayasannikarṣāt sūkṣmādiṣv asmatpratyakṣeṣu ca jñānaṃ tathaiva tatsamaveteṣu guṇakarmasu jñānamutpadyate saṃyuktasamavāyāt ||
children.translated_text: And just as, through contact of the fourfold set, cognition arises with respect to subtle things and the like, and in perceptions such as ours, so too cognition arises with respect to qualities and actions inhering in them, through inherence in what is conjoined.

children.text: yathātmamanaḥsaṃyogāt svasminnātmani jñānaṃ tathaiva svātmasamaveteṣu sukhādiṣu jñānamutpadyate ||
children.translated_text: Just as cognition arises in one's own self from the conjunction of self and mind, so too cognition arises with respect to pleasure and the like inhering in one's own self.
Having explained yogic perception, he explains inference.

children.text: asyedamiti sambandhamātraṃ darśayitvā kāryaṃ kāraṇam ityādinā viśinaṣṭi ||
children.translated_text: After indicating merely the relation expressed by 'this belongs to that,' he specifies it by such expressions as effect and cause.

children.text: kāryakāraṇagrahaṇena samavāyimātropalakṣaṇājjātyāderapi grahaṇam sambandhiśabdena saṃyogino grahaṇaṃ dhūmādeḥ ||
children.translated_text: By the mention of effect and cause, since merely the inhering cause is indicated, universals and the like also are included; and by the word 'related,' what is conjoined, such as smoke, is included.
The rest has been explained in the sūtra on the conjoined and so forth.

children.text: tatra evaṃvidhaprasiddhasambandhasyārthaikadeśam asaṃdigdhaṃ paśyataḥ śeṣānuvyavasāyo yaḥ sa liṅgadarśanāt saṃjāyamāno laiṅgikam iti vṛttikāraḥ ||
children.translated_text: There, when one sees without doubt one part of an object whose relation of this kind is well known, the subsequent cognition of the remainder that arises from the perception of the sign is called inferential, according to the author of the vṛtti.

children.text: yathā kāryādismṛtisavyapekṣam anumānaṃ trikālaviṣayam atīndriyārthaṃ ca tathaiva śābdaṃ saṅketasmṛtyapekṣaṃ trikālaviṣayam atīndriyārthaṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: Just as inference, depending on the memory of an effect and so on, has the three times as its object and also has supersensible objects as its object, so too verbal cognition, depending on memory of convention, has the three times as its object and also has supersensible objects as its object.
Therefore, because it shares one and the same welfare and risk with inference, it is in effect said to be inference itself.
If one asks, 'What is a word in relation to its meaning?', that is stated.
By the words 'reason' and the like, he intends to state that it is a cause.
'Reason,' 'statement,' and 'cause' have this meaning.

children.text: evaṃ śabdaḥ kāraṇaṃ sadarthasya pratipattau liṅgaṃ kuta iti cet ||
children.translated_text: If one asks, 'How is a word, being a cause, a sign in the apprehension of a meaning?'

children.text: yathā arthasya pratipattāviyaṃ hastaceṣṭā kāraṇaṃ pratipattavyā iti vṛttasaṅketaḥ tāṃ hastaceṣṭāṃ dṛṣṭvā tataḥ śabdāt kāraṇādarthaṃ pratipadyate evam asyārthasya pratipattāvayaṃ śabdaḥ kāraṇam iti prasiddhasaṅketastataḥ śabdāt kāraṇādarthaṃ pratipadyate yathā abhinayāderapi arthaṃ pratipadyante laukikā evaṃ śabdo'rthasya saṅketavaśena vyañjakatvāt kāraṇam iti vṛttikāraḥ ||
children.translated_text: Just as, when there is an established convention that this gesture of the hand is to be understood as a cause for the apprehension of a meaning, a person sees that hand gesture and from that cause, the word-like sign, apprehends the meaning, so too, when there is a well-known convention that this word is a cause for the apprehension of this meaning, from that cause, the word, one apprehends the meaning. Just as ordinary people understand a meaning from acting and the like, so, because through convention it manifests the meaning, a word is the cause of its meaning, according to the author of the vṛtti.
In this way analogy and the other means are included.
Thus there are only two pramāṇas (means of knowledge).

children.text: pramāṇatvaṃ ca pramīyate'neneti pramāṇaṃ pramā pramāṇamiti vā ||
children.translated_text: And pramāṇa-hood belongs to that by which something is known, or else pramā means pramāṇa.
Memory is said to be an auxiliary of inference.

children.text: agnyarthino dhūmadarśanaṃ yadutpannaṃ tadapekṣādātmāntaḥkaraṇasaṃyogād viśiṣṭācca bhāvanākhyasaṃskārād yatra dhūmastatrāgniḥ iti smṛtirutpadyate ||
children.translated_text: When, for one who wants fire, the perception of smoke has arisen, then, in dependence on that and from the conjunction of the self and inner organ, and from the special disposition called bhāvanā, there arises the memory, 'Where there is smoke, there is fire.'

children.text: uparatendriyasya pralīnamanaskasyāntaḥkaraṇenaiva jñānaṃ svapnaḥ svapne'pi svapnajñānaṃ svapnāntikam tadubhayaṃ pūrvapratyayāpekṣād ātmamanaḥsaṃyogaviśeṣād bhāvanāsahāyādutpadyate ||
children.translated_text: For one whose senses have ceased and whose mind has dissolved, cognition through the inner organ alone is dream. Even in dream, dream-cognition and what belongs to dream both arise in dependence on previous cognitions, from a special conjunction of self and mind, assisted by bhāvanā.

children.text: ananubhūtārthaviṣayamapi svapnajñānaṃ śubhāśubhasūcakaṃ dharmāt caśabdād adharmācceti ||
children.translated_text: Even dream-cognition whose object has not been previously experienced is an indication of good or bad, arising from dharma and, through the word 'and,' also from adharma.
But for one who is awake:

children.text: vātādidoṣeṇopahatendriyasya pūrvarajatānubhavajanitāt saṃskārādātmamanaḥsaṃyogācca viśiṣṭād adharmāpekṣād atasmiṃstaditi jñānaṃ yathā śuktikāyāṃ rajatamiti ||
children.translated_text: For one whose senses are impaired by disorders of wind and the like, from a saṃskāra produced by a prior experience of silver and from a special conjunction of self and mind, in dependence on adharma, there arises a cognition of 'that in what is not that,' as in the cognition 'silver' in a mother-of-pearl shell.
Indeterminate cognition is like that of a southerner on seeing a camel.
That which has the character of doubt, error, indeterminate cognition, and dream is faulty and is not a pramāṇa.
That which is non-faulty, called perception and inference, is called knowledge.

children.text: tatra yalliṅganirapekṣam atītānāgatavartamāneṣu dharmādiṣvatīndriyeṣu granthairanupātteṣu devarṣīṇāṃ yat prātibhamutpadyate vijñānaṃ laukikānāṃ kadācideva śvo me bhrātā āgantā hṛdayaṃ me kathayati iti anavadhāraṇaphalaṃ kevalaṃ tarkeṇa nīyate tadārṣamityucyate ||
children.translated_text: Among these, the spontaneous cognition that arises for divine seers with respect to past, future, and present dharma and the like, which are supersensible and not taken up in treatises, without dependence on a sign, and which sometimes occurs even among ordinary people, as when one says, 'My heart tells me that my brother will come tomorrow,' has no determinate result and is reached only by reasoning; that is called ārṣa.

children.text: añjanarasāyanādi siddhānāṃ tu sūkṣmavyavahitaviprakṛṣṭārthaviṣayaṃ yadvā divyāntarikṣādinimittebhyaḥ prāṇināṃ dharmādharmavipākaparijñānaṃ tatsiddhadarśanam ||
children.translated_text: But the cognition of accomplished beings, concerning subtle, hidden, and remote objects, through collyrium, elixirs, and the like, or the knowledge of the ripening of living beings' dharma and adharma from divine, atmospheric, and other omens, is siddha-vision.

children.text: tacca pratyakṣānumānābhyāṃ na bhidyate ārṣaṃ bhidyata iti varṇayanti ||
children.translated_text: They explain that this does not differ from perception and inference, while ārṣa does differ.
And this ārṣa cognition and siddha-vision arise from special dharma and from the conjunction of self and mind.

children.text: ātmanyeva yaḥ samavāyaḥ sukhaduḥkhayor asau pañcabhyaḥ kṣityādibhyastadāśrayibhyaśca guṇebhyo gandharasarūpasparśebhyo 'rthāntaratve hetuḥ anyaguṇānām anyatrāsamavāyāt ||
children.translated_text: The very <s>samavāya</s> (inherence) that pleasure and pain have in the self is the reason why they are different entities from the five elements beginning with earth, in which they do not reside, and from the qualities residing in those elements, namely smell, taste, color, and touch, since the qualities of one thing do not inhere in another.
And these two inhere in the self, because they form one sentence with ego-consciousness.
Even though they inhere in the self:
Pleasure is produced by causes such as women and the like.
Pain is produced by causes such as poison and the like.
And pleasure and pain are mutually opposed, because they arise through the destruction of one another.
Therefore these two are different; they are not one, even though they inhere in one and the same object.

children.text: saṃśayanirṇayau parasparābhāvamātram na vastusantāviti cen na ||
children.translated_text: If it is said that doubt and ascertainment are merely the mutual absence of one another and are not real existents, that is not so.

children.text: arthāntarāt parasparavilakṣaṇāt kāraṇād bhāva utpattiḥ saṃśayanirṇayayoḥ ||
children.translated_text: Doubt and ascertainment arise as positive states from causes that are distinct entities and mutually different.

children.text: tathāhi viśeṣaṃ jijñāsor agṛhītaviśeṣasya sāmānyālocanāt saṃśayo jāyate ||
children.translated_text: For example, doubt arises when someone who wants to know a particular distinction, but has not grasped that distinction, attends only to the general feature.
After doubt, from grasping the particular distinction by another means of knowledge,
there is the ascertainment, 'This is certainly a stump.'

children.text: yadi caitau na vastusantau bhavetāṃ naitau vilakṣaṇakāraṇābhyāmutpadyeyātām ||
children.translated_text: And if these two were not real existents, they would not arise from two different causes.

children.text: ato jñānāntarabhūtau saṃśayanirṇayau parasparataḥ nirṇayastu pratyakṣānumānābhyāṃ na bhidyata iti kecit ||
children.translated_text: Therefore doubt and ascertainment are cognitions distinct from one another. But some say that ascertainment is not different from perception and inference.

children.text: yathā smṛtimata ātmanaḥ pratyakṣaṃ liṅgaṃ dṛṣṭvā apratyakṣe jñānamutpadyate tathaiva sāmānyamātradarśanāt smṛtimato viśeṣaṃ jijñāsoragṛhīte viśeṣe sthāṇuḥ puruṣo vā iti jāyate saṃśayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Just as, for a self endowed with memory, cognition of an imperceptible object arises after seeing a perceptible sign, so too, from seeing only the general feature, doubt arises for a person who has memory, who wants to know the particular, and who has not grasped the particular: 'Is it a stump or a man?'

children.text: yathā ca bhūtārthasambandhavaśena ayam evaṃbhūto'rthaḥ iti pratyakṣamutpadyate tathaiva viśeṣasambandhavaśena nivṛtte saṃśaye idamevaṃbhūtam iti nirṇayo jāyate ||
children.translated_text: And just as perception arises, through the force of relation to a real object, in the form 'this object is of such a kind,' so too, when doubt has ceased through the force of relation to the particular, ascertainment arises in the form 'this is of such a kind.'
Now he examines cognitions of effect and cause.

children.text: svakāraṇebhya utpanne kārye bhūtaṃ niṣpannamidaṃ kāryam iti kāryajñānam viśeṣaṇajñānād viśeṣyajñānam iti nyāyena tad vyākhyātam tacca mukhyam ||
children.translated_text: When an effect has arisen from its own causes, the cognition of an effect is 'this effect has become, has been accomplished.' This is explained by the principle that knowledge of the qualified object comes from knowledge of the qualifier; and this cognition is primary.
But elsewhere it is figurative, because the effect is absent.
For example, with regard to an effect that is about to be produced:

children.text: yathābhūtāyāḥ sāmagryā anantaraṃ paṭādi kāryamutpannaṃ dṛṣṭaṃ tathābhūtasāmagrīdarśanād idānīm anutpanne'pi kārye kāryaśabdamupacarya bhaviṣyati kāryam iti jāyate kāryabuddhiḥ ||
children.translated_text: When an effect such as a cloth has been seen to arise immediately after a causal complex of a certain kind, then, from seeing a causal complex of that same kind, even while the effect has not yet arisen, the word 'effect' is applied figuratively and the cognition of an effect arises: 'the effect will come to be.'
Also with regard to an effect that is in the process of being produced:

children.text: yadā prastāritāṃstantūn pūrvapūrvasaṃyogāpekṣān upalabhamānaḥ paścāt paścāduttarottaratantusaṃyoge sati anapekṣānupalabhate tadāsya paṭṭikādyavāntaraṃ kāryaṃ paśyata utpadyamāne kāryadravye niṣpannāniṣpannasaṃyogaparyālocanayā bhavati kāryam utpadyate kāryam iti jāyate buddhiḥ ||
children.translated_text: When someone, observing stretched threads that depend on earlier and earlier conjunctions, then observes them as no longer depending on those when later and later subsequent threads are conjoined, then, while seeing an intermediate effect such as a strip of cloth, and while the effected substance is coming into being, there arises in him, through consideration of completed and uncompleted conjunctions, the cognition, 'the effect is coming to be; the effect is being produced.'

children.text: yathā cotpattau evaṃ vināśe'pi prayatnānantarotpattīnāṃ ghaṭādidravyāṇāṃ vināśe abhūt iti pratyayasya bhūtapratyakṣābhāvāt ityādinā kathitatvād idānīṃ pāriṇāmike śarīrādau kathyate ||
children.translated_text: As in production, so too in destruction. Since, in the destruction of substances such as pots, whose production immediately follows effort, the cognition 'it has ceased to be' has already been explained with the words 'because there is no perception of the past' and so forth, now the case of transformation in bodies and the like is stated.
There, when it has been destroyed:
'From what has ceased to be' means 'from what has been destroyed.'

children.text: pāṇipādagrīvādīnavayavān vibhaktānupalabhya vinaṣṭād asamavāyikāraṇāt saṃyogādvinaṣṭe kārye abhūtkāryaṃ śarīrākhyam iti jāyate buddhiḥ ||
children.translated_text: After observing that limbs such as hands, feet, and neck have been separated, when the effect has been destroyed because conjunction, its non-inherent cause, has been destroyed, the cognition arises: 'the effect called a body has ceased to be.'
Again, when it is being destroyed:

children.text: sati saṃyoge caśabdādasati ghātakādivināśakāraṇavyāpāre'pi keṣāṃcid grīvādyavayavānāmanivṛtte saṃyoge vibhāgācca pāṇyādīnāṃ vinivṛtte kāryasya śarīrāderasamavāyād vināśakāraṇāghrātatvena pracalitatvād vinaṣṭāvinaṣṭasaṃyogālocanena kāryaṃ naśyati iti jñānamutpadyate ||
children.translated_text: When conjunction still exists and, as implied by the word 'and,' even though the operation of a destructive cause such as a blow is absent, the conjunction of certain parts such as the neck has not ceased, while through separation the conjunction of hands and the like has ceased, the effect such as a body, no longer inhering because its non-inherent cause has been removed, is set in motion as being touched by a destructive cause; then, by observing both destroyed and undestroyed conjunctions, the cognition arises: 'the effect is perishing.'

children.text: anye tu abhūt kāryam iti vyācakṣate tadayuktaṃ tadabhiprāyeṇaiva kāryasya vinaṣṭatvāt ||
children.translated_text: Others explain it as 'the effect has ceased to be,' but that is not correct, because according to their own intention the effect is already destroyed.
And this cognition:

children.text: śarīrādau kvacidekasminnarthe yadā pāṇyādayo'vayavāḥ samavāyina upalabdhāḥ athāsya teṣu ekadeśabuddhirutpannā idānīṃ tān vibhajya vibhaktānupalabhya etasminnekadeśini abhūta kāryam iti jñānotpattiḥ ||
children.translated_text: When, in some one object such as a body, the inhering parts such as hands have been observed, and then a cognition of them as one part of it has arisen, after that, when one separates them and observes them as separated, the cognition arises with respect to this possessor of parts: 'the effect has ceased to be.'
He states what those parts are:

children.text: svasāmānyaviśeṣebhyaḥ śirastvādibhyo yeṣu jñānaṃ jāyate śirādayo 'vayavā ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The parts are the head and the like, in which cognition arises from their own universals and particulars, such as headhood and so on.
But cognition of a cause:

children.text: kāryaṃ dravyaṃ guṇān karma vā samavetaṃ dravye paśyato dravyaṃ kāraṇam iti mukhyā buddhiḥ kāryasya jātatvāt ||
children.translated_text: When someone sees an effect, whether a substance, a quality, or an action, inhering in a substance, the primary cognition is 'the substance is the cause,' because the effect has already arisen.
But when it has not yet arisen:

children.text: janiṣyamāṇe'pi kārye tantvādīnāṃ paraspareṇa saṃyogādasya paṭaṃ prati teṣu kāraṇabuddhirutpadyate ||
children.translated_text: Even with regard to an effect that is going to be born, because threads and the like are conjoined with one another, there arises in relation to a cloth the cognition of those threads as causes.

children.text: saṃyogavibhāgeṣu nirapekṣakāraṇatvāt tatkāraṇadravye samavetatvāt karmotpannamātrameva kāraṇabuddhiṃ janayati ||
children.translated_text: With respect to conjunctions and separations, because action is an independent cause, and because it inheres in the causal substance of those conjunctions and separations, action produces the cognition of cause immediately upon arising.
Now, with regard to qualities:

children.text: kāryarūpasya samavāyikāraṇe paṭādau yat samavāyikāraṇaṃ tantavasteṣu kāraṇakāraṇeṣu samavetatvāt kāraṇaṃ rūpādaya ityucyante caśabdādanutpanne'pi kāryarūpe kāraṇabuddhiḥ ||
children.translated_text: In the inhering cause of an effect-form, such as a cloth and the like, that inhering cause, namely the threads, is called the cause of forms and the like, because it is inherent in those causes of the cause; and by the word "and," even when the effect-form has not yet arisen, there is cognition of the cause.

children.text: kāryasya paṭādeḥ samavāyikāraṇeṣu tantvādiṣu samavetatvāt saṃyoge dravyaṃ prati kāraṇabuddhiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Because it is inherent in the inhering causes of an effect, such as threads and the like in the case of cloth and so forth, in the case of conjunction there is cognition of a substance as cause.
But at the origination of qualities and actions:

children.text: kāraṇe ghaṭe'kāraṇe cāgnāvagnisaṃyogaḥ samavetatvāt kāraṇaṃ pākajānām ||
children.translated_text: A conjunction with fire, being inherent in a causal pot and also in non-causal fire, is the cause of heat-produced qualities.

children.text: abhighātye karmakāraṇe 'bhihantari cākāraṇe samavetatvād vegavaddravyasaṃyogaḥ karmaṇaḥ kāraṇam ||
children.translated_text: A conjunction with a substance possessing velocity, because it is inherent in the struck object, which is the cause of the action, and also in the striker, which is not the cause, is the cause of action.
But at the origination of heat-produced qualities:

children.text: aṇūnāṃ pākajarūpādyārambhe'ṇubhiḥ saṃyukte'gnau samavetamuṣṇasparśaṃ vaiśeṣikaṃ guṇam apekṣate saṃyogaḥ ||
children.translated_text: In the origination of heat-produced form and the like in atoms, the conjunction depends on the distinctive quality, namely hot touch, which is inherent in the fire conjoined with the atoms.
Except in the case of substance, conjunction is a cause that depends on something else.
With regard to a supersensible object, such as an element and the like:

children.text: laiṅgikaṃ parokṣamucyate bhaviṣyati ityādi kāryāṇāṃ yenāvagamyate tadanumānaṃ pramāṇaṃ vyākhyātam ||
children.translated_text: The inferential is called indirect. That by which future and other effects are understood is inference, and inference as a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of knowledge) has been explained.

children.text: śāstrādau dharmo vyākhyeyatayā pratijñātaḥ atastasya pratyāmnāyānusaṃdhānārthaṃ sūtradvayaṃ gatamapi punarucyate ||
children.translated_text: At the beginning of the treatise, <s>dharma</s> was stated as what was to be explained. Therefore, in order to connect back with the authoritative tradition concerning it, the two sūtras, though already passed over, are stated again.

children.text: śrutau smṛtau ca dṛṣṭānāṃ dṛṣṭasya prayojanasyābhāve prayogo'bhyudayāya dharmāyetyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: When no visible purpose is found for acts seen in the <s>śruti</s> and <s>smṛti</s>, their performance is for prosperity, that is, for <s>dharma</s>.
And it has been said that knowledge of that comes from the <s>āmnāya</s> (sacred tradition).
And the authority of the <s>āmnāya</s> is established.

children.text: tanubhuvanādikāryatayā vijñāto bhagavān īśvaraḥ tatpraṇayanāccāmnāyasya siddhaṃ prāmāṇyam ||
children.translated_text: <s>Bhagavān Īśvara</s> is known from the fact that the body, the world, and so on are effects; and because the <s>āmnāya</s> was composed by him, the authority of the <s>āmnāya</s> is established.
The word "iti" indicates completion.

children.text: evaṃ dravyādīnāṃ sādharmyavaidharmyaparijñānād vairāgyadvāreṇa jñānotpatteḥ ātmā jñātavyaḥ ityādivākyebhyaścopāsākrameṇa vijñānāvāpterniḥśreyasādhigamaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus, from knowledge arising through the recognition of the similarities and dissimilarities of substances and the rest, by way of detachment, and also from statements such as "the self is to be known," attainment of the highest good occurs through the sequence of meditation.
He who is always a moon bringing joy to this world in the night of knowledge,
that <s>Candrānanda</s>, bringing joy, composed this vṛtti.
